findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.4 - SEND - Post 16 Travel Support - IIA
findings.headline: The number of families choosing a Personal Travel Budget rose from 122 in 2024/25 to 147 in 2025/26, an increase of approximately 20%.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the rise to an improved PTB offer and clearer payment bands based on journey distance. It notes that this does not show a PTB will suit every pupil or family.
findings.matters: Rising PTB take-up changes the mix between cash payments and commissioned transport, which affects how savings from the proposed options would be realised.
findings.figures: PTB families: 122 (2024/25) to 147 (2025/26), approximately 20%. In 2026/27, 35 pupils receive a PTB and 174 use commissioned transport.
findings.quote: the number of families choosing a PTB increased from 122 in 2024/25 to 147 in 2025/26, an increase of approximately 20%.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.4 - SEND - Post 16 Travel Support - IIA
findings.headline: The 2025 consultation on the revised post-16 SEND transport policy drew 50 responses, which the paper describes as mainly negative towards the proposed changes.
findings.detail: Key concerns included barriers to education for young people with SEND, families' extra costs, and a lack of clarity on eligibility and exceptional circumstances. Some respondents supported greater flexibility and targeting resources at the greatest need.
findings.matters: A council that has previously received a mainly negative response to a savings proposal, and is consulting again, shows the political and consultation risk attached to SEND transport changes.
findings.figures: 2025 consultation: 50 responses (23 online, 17 emails, nine drop-in sessions, one voicemail).
findings.quote: The 2025 consultation showed a mainly negative response to the proposed changes.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.4 - SEND - Post 16 Travel Support - IIA
findings.headline: The proposed change is to start from September 2027, one year later than the September 2026 start in the policy presented to Cabinet in October 2025.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2025 consultation informed a policy that proposed a more individualised approach from September 2026. The current proposal is to phase in a chosen approach from September 2027, after a further consultation.
findings.matters: A later start date pushes back the timing of any saving, and a finance officer tracking the planned phasing would need to adjust the profile.
findings.figures: Start dates: September 2026 (October 2025 Cabinet policy); September 2027 (current proposal). Consultation: 17 November to 29 December 2026.
findings.quote: We are considering changes to our post-16 SEND travel support offer from September 2027.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.4 - SEND - Post 16 Travel Support - IIA
findings.headline: Option 4's modelled savings rise from £860,699 in 2027/28 to £1,998,662 in 2030/31, the largest of the four options in both years.
findings.detail: Option 4 would phase in an end to routine access to commissioned transport and Personal Travel Budgets, with individual applications still assessed where the law requires. The paper says the modelling includes pupil numbers, leavers, new applicants, increased PTB use and inflation.
findings.matters: The gap between the highest-saving option and the others shows how much a phased exit from routine commissioned transport would change the cost base, which other councils facing similar transport spend would want to compare.
findings.quote: Option 4: £860,699 rising to £1,998,662.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.4 - SEND - Post 16 Travel Support - IIA
findings.headline: Four options for post-16 SEND travel support carry modelled 2027/28 savings of £228,485 to £860,699, and no saving has yet been agreed.
findings.detail: The paper states that no option has been selected and that the figures are modelled potential savings, not guaranteed ones. Savings must be adjusted for consultation outcomes, statutory provision, exceptions, retained transport, appeals and implementation costs.
findings.matters: A finance director planning a SEND transport saving needs to know that the modelled figure is not yet agreed and depends on several adjustments that have not been made.
findings.figures: 2027/28 modelled savings: Option 1 £228,485; Option 2 £622,837; Option 3 £325,333; Option 4 £860,699. Gross expenditure £1,434,266.08.
findings.quote: No saving has yet been agreed.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.2 SGO Pathways and Support IIA 2027-28
findings.headline: The paper gives external residential placements for children in care a gross expenditure of £14.9 million in 2025/26 and a net budget of £11.9 million for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The proposals are intended to reduce the number of children in external residential placements by reunification and kinship support. The paper gives the 2025/26 gross income as £2.0 million.
findings.matters: The residential budget is the baseline against which the proposal's savings are meant to be measured.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure 2025/26: £14.9 million; gross income 2025/26: £2.0 million; net budget 2026/27: £11.9 million
findings.quote: The spend below sets out the amount that the council spends on external residential placements for children in our care.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.2 SGO Pathways and Support IIA 2027-28
findings.headline: The paper states that Family Network Support Packages and wider kinship care are funded from the budget previously allocated to kinship carer allowances.
findings.detail: The paper describes this funding arrangement as offset funding. It is the mechanism that pays for the wider kinship offer without new budget.
findings.matters: Funding new support from an existing allowance budget is a reallocation that other councils running similar offers would need to account for.
findings.quote: FNSPs and Wider kinship care are funded by the budget had been allocated to pay for allowances for kinship carers – this is known as offset funding.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.2 SGO Pathways and Support IIA 2027-28
findings.headline: 234 carers supporting 328 children have applied for the enhanced kinship allowance, with a further 75 still being supported to understand the benefits.
findings.detail: The paper says all existing kinship carers receiving an allowance were contacted about the new allowance. Applications are being supported by kinship team social workers and resource workers.
findings.matters: Take-up of the enhanced allowance drives the cost of the scheme, so the application count is the measure a finance officer would track against budget.
findings.figures: 234 carers; 328 children; a further 75
findings.quote: To date, 234 carers supporting 328 children have applied for the allowances.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.2 SGO Pathways and Support IIA 2027-28
findings.headline: The paper records kinship allowance spend of approximately £2.7m per year before the DfE-funded Kinship Zone pilot began on 1 April 2026.
findings.detail: Newcastle is one of seven authorities in the national Kinship Zone pilot, which the paper says is funded by the Department for Education. Stakeholder feedback recorded in the paper includes concerns about what happens to kinship allowances when the pilot ends.
findings.matters: Allowance costs now depend on an externally funded pilot, and the paper records open questions about the position once it ends.
findings.figures: approximately £2.7m per year (kinship allowances, before the Kinship Zone pilot)
findings.quote: The budget spend on Kinship allowances prior to start of the Kinship Zone pilot on 1st April 2026, was approximately £2.7m per year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 15.2 SGO Pathways and Support IIA 2027-28
findings.headline: The paper projects net revenue savings of £381,000 in 2027/28 and £390,000 in 2028/29, with £0 in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The financial impacts section gives net revenue savings for each year of the proposal. The paper states no net income and no reduction in full-time equivalent posts.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, can compare this stated savings profile against the outcome of the external residential reduction it is tied to.

findings.headline: The external review found Newcastle's SEND transport service 'generally well run', using technology effectively and with relatively few single-passenger journeys.
findings.detail: The paper presents this as a finding from the review, alongside the opportunities it identified to improve the service and maintain its sustainability as demand grows.
findings.matters: The review's view of the service's current operation is the basis for the council's stated approach and indicates the scale of change the council is considering.
findings.quote: The review found that Newcastle’s SEND transport service is generally well run, uses technology effectively and has relatively few single-passenger journeys.

findings.headline: Gross expenditure on passenger transport is £10,376,210.74 against £90,000 of gross income, giving a net budget of £10,286,210.
findings.detail: The figures are given in the section on current spending. The paper states 1,336 students are eligible for SEND transport, of whom 1,086 are pre-16 and 250 post-16.
findings.matters: The baseline spend and eligible numbers are the denominator against which the savings targets and cost-per-pupil comparisons can be tested.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure £10,376,210.74; gross income £90,000; net budget £10,286,210; 1,336 eligible students
findings.quote: Gross expenditure: £10,376,210.74

findings.headline: 83% of SEND routes have a Passenger Assistant, against a review benchmark of 62%.
findings.detail: The review recommended reviewing how Passenger Assistant support is allocated. The paper lists this as one of seven workstreams, which include a review of the current use of escorts on transport routes.
findings.matters: Escort provision is a per-route cost that directly affects transport spend, and the gap to benchmark gives other councils a comparable measure.
findings.figures: 83% of SEND routes have a Passenger Assistant; benchmark 62%
findings.quote: 83% of SEND routes have a Passenger Assistant, compared with its benchmark of 62%.

findings.headline: 58% of children and young people with an EHCP receive transport, against a review benchmark of 38%.
findings.detail: The review recommended examining how eligibility decisions are made. The paper gives no figures for the cost effect of moving towards the benchmark.
findings.matters: The gap between the actual take-up rate and the benchmark is the main lever the council identifies for controlling SEND transport demand, and it is comparable across councils.
findings.figures: 58% of EHCP children and young people receive transport; benchmark 38%
findings.quote: 58% of children and young people with an EHCP receive transport, compared with its benchmark of 38%.

findings.headline: Consultancy modelling projects SEND transport expenditure could exceed £15 million by 2031/32, before inflation, without further intervention.
findings.detail: The external review's modelling is the basis for the proposal. The paper says costs are likely to rise with demand if no action is taken, and it links this to continued growth in Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs).
findings.matters: A forward cost projection of this kind for a statutory SEND service is a pressure that other councils' finance teams are likely to be modelling for their own budgets.
findings.figures: £15 million by 2031/32, before inflation; net budget £10,286,210
findings.quote: expenditure could exceed £15 million by 2031/32, before inflation

findings.headline: Newcastle's proposal sets net revenue savings of £584,000 in 26/27, £385,000 in 27/28 and £285,000 in 28/29 on SEND transport.
findings.detail: The paper gives a net revenue savings profile for three years and states that net income is £0. The comments say the council is exploring ways to reduce commissioned transport costs, avoid future costs and use vehicles more effectively.
findings.matters: A finance director at Newcastle or another council can compare a stated savings profile for a high-cost statutory service against the net budget it is drawn from.

findings.headline: Newcastle is consulting on five Council Tax Support changes, including raising the capital limit from £6,000 to £8,000.
findings.detail: The paper lists the proposed changes: the capital limit increase, full disregard of the LCWRA element of Universal Credit, disregard of Carer's Allowance, disregard of the Disabled Child Element of Universal Credit, and an Exceptional Hardship provision of up to 100% of the Council Tax bill. The paper does not state the cost of these changes.
findings.matters: Changes to council tax reduction rules can reduce the billable base, and a finance director would expect the cost to be quantified in the budget report.
findings.quote: increase the capital limit from £6,000 to £8,000;

findings.headline: The Council Tax base is 74,125 Band D equivalents for 2026-27, with a long-term collection rate of 98.0%.
findings.detail: The paper states that the council tax base and collection rate determine how much Council Tax is collected. It lists new properties, demolitions, and discounts, exemptions, premiums and reliefs as factors that will change the 2027-28 yield. The paper gives the 2026-27 base and collection rate as the starting assumptions.
findings.matters: The collection rate and base assumptions drive the yield from any rate rise, so a finance director can check whether the proposed £4.9 million and £3.3 million figures rest on the same base.
findings.figures: 74,125 Band D equivalents, 98.0%
findings.quote: The long-term collection rate in 2026-27 was set at 98.0%.

findings.headline: The combined proposed Council Tax rise is 4.99%, with Band D rising by £110.84 a year excluding police and fire precepts.
findings.detail: The paper combines the 2.99% core increase and the 2% adult social care precept. Its table shows Band D moving from £2,221.21 to £2,332.05 in the charge excluding police and fire precepts. The Band D charge for 2026-27 including police and fire was £2,540.66.
findings.matters: The combined rate and the Band D figure are the numbers residents see and the base against which other councils will compare their own increases.
findings.quote: The table below shows the weekly impact of the combined 4.99% increase

findings.headline: Newcastle proposes to apply the 2% adult social care precept, which it says will generate £3.3 million.
findings.detail: The paper proposes using the government's 2% adult social care precept to help fund rising adult social care demand and cost. The precept income must be used for adult social care. The paper links the precept to the long-standing impact of COVID-19 on social care services.
findings.matters: The precept is ring-fenced to adult social care, so its yield matters to finance officers judging how much of the social care budget Council Tax funds.
findings.figures: 2%, £3.3 million
findings.quote: This will generate an additional £3.3 million of Council Tax income

findings.headline: Newcastle proposes a 2.99% core Council Tax increase for 2027-28, which it expects to raise £4.9 million.
findings.detail: The paper says the council must raise more Council Tax to set a balanced 2027-28 budget. The core increase is proposed to avoid further service reductions beyond those already in the budget report. The paper expects the increase to be below the level the Secretary of State defines as excessive.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or elsewhere, can compare the size of the proposed core rise and its yield against the council's own 2027-28 budget gap and the government's 3% assumption.
findings.quote: We are proposing to increase core Council Tax by 2.99%, which will increase income by £4.9 million

findings.headline: No further Dedicated Schools Grant deficit write-off was announced in the Autumn Budget 2026, while Newcastle reports DSG pressures from more pupils eligible for SEND support
findings.detail: The paper notes the Autumn Budget provided no new funding for SEND and that no further DSG deficit write-off was announced. Within its own 2026-27 monitoring, the council reports DSG pressures driven by the increased number of pupils eligible for SEND support and the cost of meeting that support.
findings.matters: Councils with DSG deficits are watching whether national write-off support will be extended, and the absence of a further write-off in this announcement is directly relevant to their deficit planning and lending assessments.
findings.figures: No figure given for Newcastle's DSG deficit in this document
findings.quote: No further Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit write-off was announced.

findings.headline: Newcastle says the Outer West Leisure, highways and ward budget borrowing will be funded corporately through savings elsewhere in the budget
findings.detail: The paper says the Outer West Leisure project, additional highways and pavement investment, and ward capital budgets cannot generate enough income or savings to be self-financing. It says the borrowing will therefore be funded from savings elsewhere in the budget, rather than from the self-financing model used for most planned borrowing.
findings.matters: Corporately funded borrowing draws on the general budget rather than on a scheme's own income, which is a different risk profile from self-financing borrowing and is a decision other councils make for similar schemes.
findings.figures: £30.7 million Outer West Leisure Centre; £1.3 million per annum across 26 ward capital budgets at £50,000 each; £0.1 million 2027-28 budget contribution for ward budgets
findings.quote: cannot generate sufficient income or savings, and therefore must be financed by prudential borrowing funded corporately through savings elsewhere in the budget.

findings.headline: Newcastle's capital programme includes £190.0 million in 2029-30 with no funding approved yet, and £80.4 million in 2028-29
findings.detail: The paper's table of planned capital investment by source of finance shows a 'Pipeline (no funding approved yet)' line of £25.7 million in 2027-28, £80.4 million in 2028-29 and £190.0 million in 2029-30. The pipeline equals the full 2029-30 programme, with General Fund pipeline of £90.0 million and HRA pipeline of £100.0 million.
findings.matters: A multi-year capital programme largely without approved funding is a planning and borrowing exposure that lenders and finance directors at other councils would want to track as schemes are approved or dropped.
findings.figures: £25.7 million pipeline 2027-28; £80.4 million pipeline 2028-29; £190.0 million pipeline 2029-30; £202.0 million total programme 2027-28
findings.quote: Pipeline (no funding approved yet)

findings.headline: Newcastle collected 96.05% of Council Tax due in 2025-26, which the paper states was the highest amongst Core Cities
findings.detail: The paper gives a longer-term collection rate of approximately 98.11%. The council describes its Council Tax income as a growing share of its funding, rising from 19.0% to 19.5% of total General Fund income in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Strong collection rates reduce the bad-debt risk on the council's largest locally raised income stream, which is relevant to finance directors comparing collection performance and to lenders assessing revenue security.
findings.figures: 96.05% Council Tax collected in 2025-26; approximately 98.11% longer-term collection rate; 19.0% to 19.5% share of total General Fund income
findings.quote: In 2025-26 we collected 96.05% of Council Tax due, which was the highest amongst Core Cities

findings.headline: Newcastle carries a funding risk on its Recovery Grant, worth £14 million per annum, which may cease or be reduced in 2029-30
findings.detail: The paper assumes the Recovery Grant will cease in its current form and be rolled into formula funding distributed by Relative Needs, which it says would result in a potential loss of funding. The paper names this as the main reason the 2029-30 budget gap is larger than in the two preceding years.
findings.matters: A specific grant assumed to end in a named year, and the reason it drives the final-year gap, is a funding exposure other councils with similar deprivation profiles will face.
findings.figures: £14 million per annum Recovery Grant; 2029-30 funding risk; £20.8 million Better Care Grant rolled into RSG in 2027-28
findings.quote: We carry a funding risk where the Recovery Grant (worth £14 million per annum) may cease or be reduced in 2029-30.

findings.headline: Newcastle projects £110.2 million of cost pressures to 2029-30 against a £71.6 million increase in resources
findings.detail: The paper splits cost pressures into inflationary changes of £52.9 million, increasing demand of £38.8 million and other changes including headroom of £18.5 million. Choice items of £8.8 million are added, giving the £47.4 million savings requirement. Adult social care, children's social care and SEND are identified as the highest-demand areas.
findings.matters: The gap between cost growth and resource growth is the core structural pressure that finance directors elsewhere are managing, and the breakdown shows where the cost is coming from.
findings.figures: £110.2 million cost pressures to 2029-30; £52.9 million inflationary changes; £38.8 million increasing demand; £18.5 million other changes; £71.6 million increase in resources; £8.8 million choice items
findings.quote: Unfortunately, the £71.6 million increase in resources is not sufficient to keep pace with the increased costs we will face over the same period

findings.headline: Newcastle proposes using £4.0 million of reserves in its 2027-28 budget and says that use will be mainstreamed as a permanent budget requirement from 2028-29
findings.detail: The paper states the £4.0 million is £1.5 million already built into the 2026-27 base budget plus a further £2.5 million proposed for 2027-28. It says the mainstreamed reserve balances are built into the assumptions for 2028-29 and 2029-30, and that further work will try to reduce the reserve use before the January 2027 budget.
findings.matters: Using reserves to balance a recurring budget is a shift that finance directors and lenders watch closely, because the replacement cost falls into later years.
findings.figures: £4.0 million proposed reserves use in 2027-28; £1.5 million built into the 2026-27 base budget; £2.5 million further proposed for 2027-28
findings.quote: However, long-term use of reserves is not sustainable and the proposed reserves need to be funded over the duration of the MTFP.

findings.headline: Newcastle's medium-term plan shows savings required of £12.7 million in 2027-28, £13.5 million in 2028-29 and £21.2 million in 2029-30, totalling £47.4 million
findings.detail: The savings requirement rises in each year, with the largest amount in 2029-30. The paper attributes the larger 2029-30 gap mainly to the assumed change in treatment of the Recovery Grant.
findings.matters: Savings requirements that rise in the final year of the plan indicate how much of the medium-term position still depends on delivering further change, which is what peers and lenders need to judge the plan's credibility.
findings.figures: £12.7 million 2027-28; £13.5 million 2028-29; £21.2 million 2029-30; £47.4 million total over three years
findings.quote: The savings required over the next three years are £47.4 million.

findings.headline: Newcastle identifies £17.6 million of savings across 2026-27 and 2027-28 against £4.9 million brought forward and £12.7 million for 2027-28, leaving a remaining budget gap of £0.0 million
findings.detail: Table 13 sets out the proposed savings from the Change and Innovation Programme against the £4.9 million brought forward from 2026-27 and the £12.7 million estimated gap for 2027-28. The paper says the £12.7 million gap is after the proposed use of £4.0 million of reserves, and that savings are estimated and subject to detailed delivery plans.
findings.matters: A council showing a closed gap for a year on the basis of programme savings, rather than cuts alone, is a model other finance officers will compare against their own transformation plans.
findings.figures: £17.6 million estimated savings; £4.9 million budget gap brought forward; £12.7 million estimated 2027-28 budget gap; £0.0 million remaining gap; approximately 307.6 FTE reduction across 2026-27 and 2027-28
findings.quote: Remaining budget gap 0.0

findings.headline: Newcastle will need to rebuild its unearmarked General Fund reserve to £21.1 million, its assessed financial risk, as part of the 2026-27 outturn
findings.detail: The paper says a £6.1 million overspend could reduce the unearmarked reserve from £18.3 million to £12.2 million by 31 March 2027. The council's risk assessment quantifies financial risks at £21.1 million, so the council says it will need to develop options to restore the reserve to that level.
findings.matters: A reserve below the council's own risk assessment is a direct measure of its capacity to absorb unplanned pressures, which matters to finance directors benchmarking reserves and to lenders assessing resilience.
findings.figures: £18.3 million unearmarked General Fund reserve at 31 March 2026; £12.2 million potential balance at 31 March 2027; £21.1 million assessed financial risk
findings.quote: the council will need to develop options to increase the level of the unearmarked General Fund reserve back up to £21.1 million as part of the 2026-27 outturn.

findings.headline: Newcastle projects a £6.1 million General Fund overspend at Q1 2026-27, against an unearmarked General Fund reserve of £18.3 million at 31 March 2026
findings.detail: The paper reports pressures of £3.2 million in Children's & Families, £2.7 million in Adult Social Care & Prevention, £5.4 million in the Property Portfolio and £1.6 million in Legal & Governance Services, partly offset by underspends elsewhere. If the overspend is the year-end position, it would be funded from the unearmarked General Fund reserve.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the service pressures and the reserve-funded route for an in-year overspend, and a lender can see how much of the unearmarked reserve the projection would use.
findings.figures: £6.1 million projected overspend at Q1 2026-27; £3.2 million Children's & Families; £2.7 million Adult Social Care & Prevention; £5.4 million Property Portfolio; £1.6 million Legal & Governance Services; £18.3 million unearmarked General Fund reserve at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The Council is currently projecting a potential pressure at Q1 2026-27 of £6.1 million on its General Fund budget at this stage of the year.

findings.headline: Transformation reserve is shown at £19.6m at 31 March 2026 (actual), with projected balances of £13.9m at 31 March 2027, £6.4m at 31 March 2028 and nil at 31 March 2029.
findings.detail: The paper shows the Transformation reserve being drawn down across each estimate year until it reaches nil by 31 March 2029. It was the largest single movement in the table after the Revenue grants to be applied reserve. The paper does not give the purpose of the drawdowns in this appendix.
findings.matters: Council transformation programmes are usually funded from reserves, so a finance officer elsewhere would want to see how fast this council plans to draw on its transformation funding.
findings.figures: (19.6) £m at 31 March 2026 (actual); (13.9) £m at 31 March 2027 (estimate); (6.4) £m at 31 March 2028 (estimate); nil at 31 March 2029 (estimate)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 9 - Projected trend in earmarked reserves
findings.headline: Total General Fund earmarked reserves are shown at £158.8m at 31 March 2026 (actual), with estimates of £138.1m at 31 March 2027, £118.3m at 31 March 2028 and £102.8m at 31 March 2029.
findings.detail: The total row sets out the combined balance of all listed earmarked reserves across the six year-ends. The paper shows the 2026 actual as the highest figure in the series. The fall after that is the sum of the individual reserve movements in the appendix.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this projected run-down of earmarked reserves against its own plans for using reserves to fund the budget.
findings.figures: (158.8) £m at 31 March 2026 (actual); (138.1) £m at 31 March 2027 (estimate); (118.3) £m at 31 March 2028 (estimate); (102.8) £m at 31 March 2029 (estimate)

findings.matters: Lenders and finance directors compare how the net revenue budget is funded across council tax, grant and business rates, and the paper shows movement in all three.

findings.detail: Corporate Items sit below the directorate lines and are shown as a single figure for each year. The paper does not break down what the line contains.
findings.matters: Corporate items are a line a reader cannot see into from the directorate budgets, so a rise of this size changes how far the net revenue budget can be explained by service spend.
findings.figures: Corporate Items £57.963m (2026-27) and £82.727m (2027-28); Net Service Expenditure £316.798m and £331.779m

findings.detail: Gross expenditure rises from £252.685m to £257.010m. Gross income falls over the same period, and the paper shows that fall alongside the rise in net expenditure.
findings.matters: A net rise accompanied by a fall in gross income is a pattern a finance director at another council would compare against their own income assumptions for the service.
findings.figures: Gross expenditure £252.685m (2026-27) and £257.010m (2027-28); gross income £116.935m and £109.342m; net expenditure £135.750m and £147.668m

findings.detail: Gross income for the directorate rises from £190.784m to £322.937m, so most of the increase in gross spend is matched by income. The paper does not say what that income is or where it comes from.
findings.matters: Gross spend and gross income both rise by more than £130m, and a reader comparing councils needs the source of that income to judge whether it is secure.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Net expenditure budgets by directorate
findings.headline: Transfers from reserves in the net revenue budget rise from £0.846m in 2026-27 to £3.385m in 2027-28
findings.detail: The reserves line is shown in brackets in both years. The net revenue budget reconciles as net service expenditure plus corporate items, less this line (£316.798m + £57.963m − £0.846m = £373.915m for 2026-27). The column headings above the reconciliation read 2025-26 and 2026-27, but the figures reconcile to 2026-27 and 2027-28 in the directorate table.
findings.matters: A finance director, here or at another council, would want to know how far the net revenue budget depends on reserves, and that dependence is shown rising across the two years.
findings.figures: Reserves transfer £0.846m (2026-27) and £3.385m (2027-28), both shown in brackets; net revenue budget £373.915m (2026-27) and £411.121m (2027-28)

findings.headline: The Council has added a corporate risk relating to Programme delivery, and the paper says some benefit profiles have increased beyond initial projections.
findings.detail: The paper says benefits profiles are being continually refined and that workstreams are progressing well towards anticipated timelines for benefit realisation over a three-year period.
findings.matters: A corporate risk entry on programme delivery, alongside revised benefit profiles, is the kind of governance signal a finance director compares with their own transformation risk registers.
findings.quote: some have increased beyond initial projections.

findings.headline: Systems Bridge ERP has a Go Live date of end of August 2027, with an indicative saving of £0.5m and c.33 FTE workforce impact.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme is in the Explore phase, with a fit-to-standard approach and Deloitte as delivery partner alongside a third-party assurance provider. Every phase is planned against the Go Live date.
findings.matters: A finance director can track an ERP go-live date and its delivery approach, given the scale and risk of replacing core finance, HR, payroll and procurement systems.
findings.figures: Go Live end of August 2027; £0.5m indicative contribution; c.33 FTE
findings.quote: Go Live is end of August 2027.

findings.headline: More than £1m has been claimed from the Department for Education to fund enhanced kinship allowances.
findings.detail: The paper says the Kinship Zone pilot has supported 225 carers and benefited 312 children. It says the enhanced allowances give greater financial stability for kinship carers.
findings.matters: Grant income claimed against enhanced kinship allowances is an external funding source that a finance director can check against their own claims.
findings.figures: More than £1m claimed from the Department for Education; 225 carers; 312 children
findings.quote: More than £1m has been claimed from the Department for Education to fund enhanced kinship allowances

findings.headline: Newcastle's Children's Social Care expenditure budget increased from £52.83m to £54.68m between 2024 and 2026, and the Education expenditure budget increased from £8.55m to £11.86m over the same period.
findings.detail: The paper says the Children's Social Care increase was lower than in comparable local authorities and that an LGA review found the Council operates at comparatively low cost. It also says the Council has a higher number and rate of children in care than comparable authorities.
findings.matters: Budget growth in children's social care and education, alongside a higher rate of children in care, is the kind of demand pressure other finance directors are tracking against their own budgets.
findings.figures: Children's Social Care budget £52.83m to £54.68m; Education budget £8.55m to £11.86m
findings.quote: expenditure budget increased from £52.83m to £54.68m between 2024 and 2026

findings.headline: Monitoring indicates that the planned £143,000 saving for 2026/27 from Families First is on track, with placements reducing from 100 in April 2026 to 86 by March 2029.
findings.detail: The primary financial benefit is a reduction in reliance on Independent Fostering Agency placements for Children in Care. The paper says tracking of wider benefits is still being developed.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the saving and placement reduction trajectory against their own placement-led savings, including the timing of the 2026/27 figure.
findings.figures: £143,000 saving for 2026/27; placements from 100 in April 2026 to 86 by March 2029
findings.quote: monitoring indicating that the planned £143,000 saving for 2026/27 is currently on track

findings.headline: Children's SEND transport reports £584,000 delivered in 2026/27 against a target of £695,000 (84%), primarily through route optimisation.
findings.detail: The paper says the Children's Transport workstream will contribute £125,000 from Independent Travel Training, including a £25,000 saving in 2026/27 that is on track. It says the workstream will also deliver the Children and Families contribution to a separate £1.9m target over three years.
findings.matters: A finance officer tracking SEND transport savings can compare delivery against target for the year, and the route optimisation approach offers a comparison point for other councils.
findings.figures: £584,000 delivered; £695,000 target; 84%; £125,000 from Independent Travel Training; £25,000 saving in 2026/27; £1.9m three-year target
findings.quote: Current reporting indicates that £584,000 has been delivered in 2026/27 against a target of £695,000 (84%)

findings.headline: The centralised print and post budget is overspent, with a further 17% increase in Business Postage proposed.
findings.detail: The paper says demand is an issue and that Royal Mail price increases add to the pressure. Business Postage is under review by Ofcom, and the Council is reviewing all postage and promoting digital post.
findings.matters: Postage cost increases outside a council's control can add to an existing overspend, and the reduction measures show how one council is responding.
findings.figures: further 17% increase proposed in Business Postage
findings.quote: the centralised budget is currently overspent

findings.headline: The third party spend review analysed £487m of addressable third party spend across 3000+ suppliers from FY24/25, and selected five areas for deep dive.
findings.detail: The five deep-dive areas are ICT Hardware, ICT Software, Fleet, Children's Services and Adults. The paper says the next phase of deep-dive reviews is being scoped and that the workstream's financial contribution is £1.2m, profiled over a longer period to reflect contract renewal timelines.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the addressable base and the deep-dive scope against their own third-party spend analysis, and the longer profile signals when savings from contract renewals will arrive.
findings.figures: £487m addressable third party spend; 3000+ suppliers; five deep-dive areas; £1.2m indicative financial contribution
findings.quote: £487m of addressable third party spend

findings.headline: Consultation on the operating model has concluded with 7 voluntary redundancies and 5 deleted vacancies, which the paper says achieves a financial saving of £549k.
findings.detail: The paper reports that consultation has concluded for one of the Operating Model areas. It says the Council remains committed to avoiding compulsory redundancies as far as possible.
findings.matters: Realised savings from voluntary redundancy and vacancy deletion show how far a workforce saving has landed compared with the indicative figures elsewhere in the paper.
findings.figures: 7 voluntary redundancies; 5 vacancies deleted; £549k saving
findings.quote: achieving a financial saving of £549k

findings.headline: The initial six Operating Model reviews have an indicative saving of £3.0m with c.93 FTE post reductions, and four additional reviews have an indicative saving of £1.2m with c.28 FTE.
findings.detail: The four additional operating models are at stage 2 of the design process. The paper says consultation with colleagues and Trade Unions continues on these reductions.
findings.matters: The paper sets out the staffing and saving scale of a multi-function operating model review, which peers designing similar reviews can compare against.
findings.figures: £3.0m saving; c.93 FTE; further £1.2m saving; c.28 FTE
findings.quote: The indicative impact of our initial 6 Operating Model reviews is a £3.0m saving with c.93 FTE post reductions across the Council.

findings.headline: The Organisation Design review has an indicative saving of £3.5m with c.52 FTE post reductions, and a further £1.2m with c.14 FTE has been identified.
findings.detail: The paper says consultation with colleagues and Trade Unions is under way on these reductions. It expects 70% of the further FTE reductions to be achieved by deleting vacancies, subject to validation through consultation.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the scale of workforce-led savings and the share expected from vacancy deletion against their own organisational design plans.
findings.figures: £3.5m saving; c.52 FTE post reductions; further £1.2m saving; c.14 FTE; 70% of further FTE reductions expected from vacancy deletion
findings.quote: The indicative impact of our Organisation Design review is a £3.5m saving with c.52 FTE post reductions across the Council.

findings.headline: In the People's Budget simulator, Enabling & Business Functions showed the biggest percentage decrease, from £25.0M to £20.4M, while Enforcement & Regulation showed the biggest percentage increase, from £2.0M to £2.5M.
findings.detail: The figures are the average of submitted simulator budgets compared with 2026-2027 actual spend, not a council decision. The paper links this public preference to the council's Change and Innovation programme, which includes proposals to review third-party contract spending.
findings.matters: A finance director can set this public preference for back-office reduction against their own enabling-cost savings plans and third-party contract reviews, and see how public appetite for those savings is being tested.
findings.figures: £25.0M to £20.4M (Enabling & Business Functions, percentage decrease); £2.0M to £2.5M (Enforcement & Regulation, 25.0% increase)
findings.quote: the biggest percentage decrease was in Enabling & Business Functions – from 25.0M to £20.4M.

findings.headline: The People's Budget 2027-2028 simulator aggregate included a 2.9% Council Tax and Adult Social Care Precept increase, generating £5million, the maximum allowed without a referendum.
findings.detail: The paper says the 2.9% increase is the maximum without triggering a referendum and is consistent with decisions made in previous years. It also notes that the simulator did not ask about other income sources such as fees and charges this year.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the public-preferred precept assumption and its £5million yield with their own referendum-limit planning, and see that fees and charges were not tested with the public this cycle.
findings.figures: 2.9%; £5million
findings.quote: The People’s Budget for 2027-2028 had a Council Tax and Adult Social Care Precept increase of 2.9%, generating £5million.

findings.headline: The Adult Social Care directorate lists lack of sustainable funding as the key risk reported regularly to Audit Committee.
findings.detail: The paper says lack of sustainable adult social care funding is the key risk reported regularly to Audit Committee. It adds that the sector is supported by short-term ring-fenced funding pots that do not allow planning beyond 12-24 months.
findings.matters: A council naming funding sustainability as its top reported risk to audit committee is a governance signal that peers and lenders will weigh alongside their own adult social care exposure.
findings.figures: planning horizon of 12-24 months for short-term funding pots
findings.quote: Lack of sustainable funding for adult social care continues to be a major concern and is the key risk reported on a regular basis to Audit Committee.

findings.headline: Paper says the Health Determinants Research Collaboration needs a contract variation to December 2028, with 19 posts "at risk" from October 2027 without it
findings.detail: The Public Health directorate says it is seeking approval for a contract variation to extend HDRC funding until December 2028. It says the paper treats continuation as dependent on a successful application.
findings.matters: Staff at risk of redundancy tied to an external funding application is a workforce and funding dependency that other councils hosting similar collaborations will recognise.
findings.figures: 19 posts; funding extension to December 2028; posts at risk from October 2027
findings.quote: Failure to secure funding would place the HDRC team (19 posts) at risk of redundancy or redeployment from October 2027

findings.headline: The Public Health directorate reports approximately £6.3 million (around 22%) of the Public Health Grant is invested across other council directorates in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper states the Public Health Grant is on a three-year settlement covering 2026/27 to 2028/29, which it says gives greater certainty. It also says a review has strengthened assurance that grant spending across directorates meets grant conditions.
findings.matters: Ring-fenced grant funding moved into other directorates, under a three-year settlement, is a compliance and allocation exposure that peers will watch.
findings.figures: approximately £6.3 million (around 22%) of the Public Health Grant; three-year settlement 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.quote: In 2026/27, approximately £6.3 million (around 22%) of the Public Health Grant is invested across other Council directorates.

findings.headline: The paper says Extended Producer Responsibility packaging payments will be a net income to the council in the short term.
findings.detail: The City Operations directorate reports that EPR 2025 payments from packaging producers will be net income in the short term, and that council allocations have been notified. It expects the income to fall over time as packaging reduces, and notes that future Revenue Support Grant reductions may offset the gain.
findings.matters: EPR is a new income stream that could reverse over time, which finance directors modelling medium-term income will need to consider.
findings.figures: not stated in the paper
findings.quote: This will be a net income to the council in the short term

findings.headline: The paper names the Environmental Tax Scheme cost from 2028 on energy recovery facilities at £1m - £3m per year, with actual costs not yet known.
findings.detail: The City Operations directorate says Energy Recovery Facilities will be in scope of the Emissions Trading Scheme from 2028, with councils charged for fossil carbon emissions from residual waste. Actual costs are unknown, and the paper says mitigation is through diverting plastic waste into recycling.
findings.matters: A new carbon charge on waste treatment from 2028 is a cost not yet in the base budget that waste-disposal authories elsewhere will also face.
findings.figures: £1m - £3m annually; scope from 2028
findings.quote: Actual costs are as yet unknown but are expected to be in the region of £1m - £3m annually based on our current waste flows.

findings.headline: The paper says the number of children in care is higher than the national average or statistical neighbours, and that approximately 77% of children in care are in a foster placement.
findings.detail: The Children and Families directorate reports that children in care numbers are significantly higher than the national average and statistical neighbours. It says the national placement crisis has significantly increased placement costs in Newcastle, and that a small number of children require residential placements.
findings.matters: Rising looked-after numbers and placement costs are a demand-led pressure that other councils with similar cohorts will recognise.
findings.figures: approximately 77% of children in care in a foster placement
findings.quote: The number of children in care is significantly higher than the national average or statistical neighbours

findings.headline: The DfE has confirmed the High Needs Stability Grant will cover up to 90% of the DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026, and funding for the remaining deficit is not yet confirmed.
findings.detail: The paper states that the DfE has confirmed the High Needs Stability Grant covers up to 90% of the DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026. It says future funding arrangements for the remaining deficit have not been confirmed, and that the Statutory Override is due to conclude on 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: A DSG deficit with no confirmed funding for its residual balance, ahead of the override ending, is a liability a lender or peer finance director will want to track.
findings.figures: up to 90% of the total DSG deficit as at 31 March 2026; Statutory Override due to conclude 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Future funding arrangements to support the remaining DSG deficit have not yet been confirmed.

findings.headline: The nine listed general fund in-year risks total £21.1 million weighted.
findings.detail: The paper gives a total weighted impact across all nine listed risks of £21.1 million. The sum of the individual weighted impacts in the table matches this total.
findings.matters: A single aggregate weighted figure for in-year general fund risk is the number a finance director would set against reserves and contingency when judging how much headroom the budget has.
findings.figures: Total weighted impact £21.1 million across nine risks.
findings.quote: TOTAL = £21.1 million

findings.headline: Slippage in budget savings proposals and efficiency measures is put at £4.4 million potential impact, 25% likelihood, with a weighted impact of £1.1 million.
findings.detail: The table includes slippage in budget savings proposals and efficiency measures as one of the nine in-year risks. The paper gives it a 25% likelihood of occurrence.
findings.matters: Savings slippage is a direct test of whether a council's budget plan is being delivered during the year, and the paper quantifies the exposure rather than leaving it as a general caveat.
findings.figures: Potential impact £4.4 million; likelihood 25%; potential weighted impact £1.1 million.
findings.quote: measures 4.4 25% 1.1

findings.headline: A shortfall in costs recovered from third parties and the capital programme is put at £9.4 million potential impact, 35% likelihood, with a weighted impact of £3.3 million.
findings.detail: The paper lists a shortfall in costs recovered from third parties and the capital programme as the second-largest weighted risk in the table. The recovery shortfall is a reduction in income the general fund expects to receive from those sources.
findings.matters: Recharges to the capital programme and third-party cost recovery are a common general fund pressure, and the size of this line shows how far a council's revenue position depends on recovering costs from elsewhere.
findings.figures: Potential impact £9.4 million; likelihood 35%; potential weighted impact £3.3 million.
findings.quote: programme 9.4 35% 3.3

findings.headline: The children's social care placement budget carries a £3.5 million potential cost pressure at 75% likelihood, the highest likelihood of the nine listed risks, with a weighted impact of £2.6 million.
findings.detail: The table shows a cost pressure on the children's social care placement budget at a 75% likelihood of occurrence. This is the highest likelihood percentage in the table, although its potential impact is smaller than the adult social care item.
findings.matters: A high likelihood on a children's placement budget indicates the council's own assessment that this pressure is more likely than not to crystallise in the year, which is relevant to peers managing the same statutory demand.
findings.figures: Potential impact £3.5 million; likelihood 75%; potential weighted impact £2.6 million.
findings.quote: Cost pressure on children's social care placement budget 3.5 75% 2.6

findings.headline: The adult social care placement budget carries a £12.5 million potential cost pressure at 50% likelihood, a weighted impact of £6.3 million, the largest of the nine listed risks.
findings.detail: The risk assessment lists a cost pressure on the adult social care placement budget as the largest item in the table. The paper gives it a 50% likelihood of occurrence.
findings.matters: Adult social care placement costs are the largest single weighted in-year risk in the table, so a finance director elsewhere can compare how much of their own general fund exposure sits in the same budget line.
findings.figures: Potential impact £12.5 million; likelihood 50%; potential weighted impact £6.3 million.
findings.quote: Cost pressure on adult social care placement budget 12.5 50% 6.3

findings.headline: Pay inflation pressure of £7.0m in 2027-28 is an estimate based on previous pay awards, pending the national pay agreement
findings.detail: The paper says the cost is an estimate from previous years' pay awards and that the actual cost will be set by the pay award agreed through national pay bargaining. The council states there is no mitigation for this pressure and no underspend to absorb it.
findings.matters: A pay pressure that depends on a national settlement not yet agreed is one that finance directors across English councils are also budgeting against, and its size depends on that outcome.
findings.quote: The cost pressure is an estimate based on the cost of previous years’ pay awards – the actual cost will be determined by the pay award agreed as part of the national pay agreement process.

findings.headline: Food waste collections from April 2026 are cited as a legal requirement behind part of the £2.5m other services demand pressure
findings.detail: The other services demand pressure is partly based on the projected increase in children with Education, Health and Care Plans and partly on wider demand, including the introduction of food waste collections. The council says the food waste collection is a legal requirement from April 2026.
findings.matters: A new statutory service cost arising from a dated legal requirement is a cost other councils with the same April 2026 duty will also face, and it is a cost the council says it cannot avoid.
findings.quote: The requirement to introduce food waste collections from April 2026.

findings.headline: Social care increased demand is put at £12.4m in 2027-28, rising from population growth and more intensive support
findings.detail: The paper attributes the pressure to increasing population and demand for more intensive support arrangements in adult and children's social care. It is based on assumed growth in the number of service users applied to current projected expenditure, and the council says the activity is a statutory duty.
findings.matters: Social care demand is the largest single demand line in the paper, and the council's basis for it (projected service user growth) is one that other councils and lenders can compare with their own forecasts.
findings.quote: Increasing demand arising from increasing population and an increasing demand for more intensive support arrangements.

findings.headline: £4.0m of reserves is proposed to be used within the 2027-28 budget
findings.detail: The paper says £4.0m use of reserves is proposed within the 2027-28 budget. It also says the pressure includes the need to fund areas of the budget from permanent resources that were previously funded through reserves.
findings.matters: Drawing reserves to balance a year's budget, and then having to replace that funding from permanent resources, is a change in the council's reserve position that finance officers elsewhere will track.
findings.figures: £4.0m use of reserves (2027-28); £9.0m total for changes in government grants, use of reserves and other pressures (2027-28)
findings.quote: £4.0 million use of reserves is proposed within the 2027-28 budget.

findings.headline: The council says it has no underspends that can absorb the £10.4m social care inflation pressure in 2027-28
findings.detail: The social care inflation pressure is based on assumed increases in hourly rates payable to third parties, including the National Living Wage. The council states there are no underspends in the budget that can absorb the pressure and that, if funding is not agreed, it will overspend.
findings.matters: A council stating that it has no underspend to absorb a pressure, and that it would overspend without funding, is a direct statement of its own budget headroom that peers and lenders can measure against their own.
findings.quote: No, there are no underspends in the budget that can absorb this pressure.

findings.headline: Cost pressures total £46.3m in 2027-28, £29.3m in 2028-29 and £34.6m in 2029-30
findings.detail: The table sets out pay, price, contractual, demand and other pressures for each year. The 2027-28 figure is the largest, and the paper's section on other pressures includes a £9.0m line for 2027-28 that is linked to government grant changes and the use of reserves.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size and make-up of these pressures with its own medium-term plan, and a lender can see the scale of the gap the council is planning to close.

findings.headline: Connect to Work grant of £2.7 million from the Department for Work and Pensions funds the Supported Employment Service through to March 2030
findings.detail: The paper reports that the council has received £2.7 million from the Department for Work and Pensions to expand its Supported Employment Service. It says 40 people have moved into work to date.
findings.matters: External funding that runs to a fixed date with a defined amount is relevant to a finance director planning service funding beyond the current year.
findings.figures: £2.7 million; 40 people moved into work; funding through March 2030
findings.quote: We have received £2.7 million to expand

findings.headline: Transformation Programme is a new Amber priority 9 strategic risk, with the Change and Innovation Newcastle Programme cited
findings.detail: The paper adds a new Amber risk on the Transformation Programme. The risk states that without sustained stakeholder alignment, sufficient resourcing and a clear scope, the programme may not deliver its intended impact. The risk description refers to long-term financial sustainability as one of the intended outcomes.
findings.matters: A finance director would see a council recording a new risk that its savings and transformation programme may not deliver long-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: Amber 9 New risk
findings.quote: Change and Innovation Newcastle Programme may not achieve its intended cross-council transformational impact

findings.headline: Bed and breakfast and hotel nights used for homelessness rose to 651 in Quarter 2 from 246 in Quarter 1
findings.detail: The paper states that 2026-27 is the first year since 2006 that the council has needed bed and breakfast and hotel use to meet homelessness duties. It reports a 164.6% increase, or 405 additional nights, between the two quarters.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a demand pressure that finance officers at other councils track closely, and the paper gives the nights and the percentage change.
findings.figures: 651 nights in Quarter 2; 246 nights in Quarter 1; 164.6% increase; 405 additional nights
findings.quote: 2026-27 is the first year since 2006 that we have needed to use bed and breakfast

findings.headline: In-year business rates collection was 55.6% at the end of September, below the same point last year but above the profiled target
findings.detail: The paper says business rates collection is below last year's figure at the same point. It says the collection remains above the profiled target. The paper links the position to legislative changes on 1 April 2026 that delayed some bills and created instalment schedules running from June 2026.
findings.matters: Business rates timing changes affect in-year cash flow, and the same legislative change may apply to other councils in England.
findings.figures: 55.6% in-year collection at end of September; year-end target 98.6%

findings.headline: Children's and Families Newcastle is overspending by £2.521 million due to increased placement costs.
findings.detail: The overspend reflects increased numbers and costs of external fostering placements, external residential placements, and services for children with disabilities, plus higher staffing costs for in-house residential services. The paper notes "There have been additional placements starting since the outturn of 2025/26," indicating this is volume-driven. SEN services contribute an additional £0.740m overspend within the directorate.
findings.matters: Child placement costs are driven by real need (children in crisis) and are difficult to control without reducing service provision. Growing placement numbers signal either more children in crisis or earlier intervention, both of which create ongoing budget pressure.
findings.figures: £2.521 million in Children's placement costs; £3.228 million total directorate overspend
findings.quote: Children's and Families Newcastle, which is projecting an overspend of £2.521 million due mainly to increased costs of providing services to children in care, especially external fostering placements, external residential placements, children with disabilities and increased costs of staffing in-house residential services.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care Community Support is overspending by £5.273 million due to demand for learning disability and dementia care.
findings.detail: Within the directorate's £2.688m overspend, Community Support alone is £5.273m over budget. This is driven by increased numbers of clients requiring nursing care, residential care, home care, and "an increase in clients needing more complex and costly dementia support packages." Other ASC services are underspent (Care & Support -£0.476m, Prevention -£1.447m, QS&I -£0.632m), but demand in Community Support dominates.
findings.matters: Demand-driven social care overspends are structural—they reflect real demographic and health needs, not operational inefficiency, and are difficult to reverse without restricting access. This signals ongoing budget pressure that may persist and grow.
findings.figures: £5.273 million overspend in Community Support; £2.688 million directorate overspend
findings.quote: Community Support, which is projecting an overspend of £5.273 million due mainly to high demand for learning disability commissioned services. findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block deficit is growing to £17.153 million, with the council dependent on government support by 2028.
findings.detail: The DSG reserve stood at negative £5.808m on 1 April 2026. High Needs spend is forecast at £66.6m against funding of £55.2m (15% spending growth vs 7% funding growth). The cumulative deficit will reach £17.153m by year-end. This is currently covered by a statutory override extending to March 2028, so it is not immediately impacting the General Fund. However, the override expires in 2028, creating a financial cliff. The government is offering a High Needs Stability Grant (up to 90% of eligible deficits), but this is conditional on Department for Education approval of a SEND reform plan—an uncertain dependency.
findings.matters: Although currently overridden, the DSG deficit represents a £17m+ structural liability that will transfer to the General Fund unless government support is approved. The 2028 override expiration creates a known deadline for financial stress, and the council's ability to manage this depends on external grant approval.
findings.figures: £11.297 million overspend in 2026-27; cumulative DSG reserve deficit £17.153 million; DSG reserve negative £5.808 million at 1 April 2026; High Needs spend £66.6m vs funding £55.2m
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) is projecting an overspend of £11.297 million. Currently, the Council can account for this as an unusable reserve due to a statutory override... This was due to expire in March 2026 however government has announced an extension to March 2028.

findings.matters: Property portfolio management is critical to council finances. findings.headline: Housing complaints doubled to 1,062 in 2025/26 while tenant satisfaction with complaints handling remains at only 31.8%
findings.detail: Complaints increased by 113.7% from 497 in 2024/25 to 1,062 in 2025/26. The council attributes this to proactive awareness-raising through 'Getting to Know You Visits' and considers it planned and welcomed. However, tenant satisfaction with complaints handling of only 31.8% (though improved from 21.1%) suggests sustained underlying service concerns requiring ongoing management.
findings.matters: Sustained low satisfaction combined with doubled complaint volumes signals potential service delivery issues that could affect housing revenue, tenant retention, or arrears management
findings.figures: 497 complaints in 2024/25; 1,062 in 2025/26 (113.7% increase); tenant satisfaction 31.8% in 2025/26 vs 21.1% in 2024/25

findings.headline: Housing complaint handling identified as not fully compliant with the Housing Ombudsman's statutory Complaints Handling Code
findings.detail: The council's regulatory action plan identifies that the housing complaint handling process is not fully compliant with the Complaints Handling Code (a statutory requirement since 1 April 2024). Non-compliance creates risk of Complaint Handling Failure Notice or Order from the Housing Ombudsman, which are published in the Ombudsman's Annual Complaints Review and shared with the Regulator of Social Housing. The Ombudsman can also refer to the Regulator if it suspects systematic failure.
findings.matters: Regulatory enforcement action and potential regulator referral are published and could trigger formal intervention affecting the council's standing and lending capacity
findings.figures: In 2025/26, council received 1,062 complaints (113.7% increase from 497 in 2024/25); only 31.8% of tenants satisfied with complaints handling
findings.quote: Our regulatory action plan is presented to Cabinet and progress updated quarterly. This plan identifies that the housing complaint handling process is not fully compliant and although our most recent tenant satisfaction measures highlight how we are improving handling complaints we are still under performing.

Caused by £3.9 million pressure from increased costs of external residential placements and in-house residential staffing, plus £2.5 million in Education (SEN transport costs and growing demand for Education Psychology Service). Q1 2025/26 forecast shows council-wide overspend of £5.5 million, suggesting continued pressure. This reflects sector-wide growth in Children's Services costs.
findings.matters: Recurring overspend in Children's Services indicates underlying costs are rising faster than budget provision. This is a sector-wide issue but this council shows consistent pressure, suggesting the £62.7 million three-year savings target will be harder to achieve and may require either greater savings elsewhere or increased borrowing.
findings.figures: £6.3 million Children & Families overspend 2024/25; £3.9 million on children in care; £2.5 million in Education; £5.5 million council-wide forecast overspend Q1 2025/26
findings.quote: The most significant budget variance was in Children & Families, where the directorate overspent by £6.3 million in year. The outturn report refers to this being caused by: - £3.9 million pressure on Children's Social Care mainly due to increased costs of providing services to children in care, especially external residential placements

findings.paper_title: 9.2.1 Appendix A 25 NCC Auditor's Annual Report FINAL
findings.headline: Regulator for Social Housing assigned C3 rating for serious failings in council's 24,000 rented properties; 2,000+ damp and mould cases unresolved.
findings.detail: On 15 January 2025, the Regulator for Social Housing assessed Newcastle's housing service as C3, meaning 'serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvement is needed'. The council identified 16 areas falling short of regulatory requirements (safety, rent issues), with a backlog of over 2,000 damp and mould cases and no up-to-date stock condition survey. The council brought housing services in-house from subsidiary Your Homes Newcastle in July 2024. A three-year recovery plan with quarterly Cabinet reporting is in place.
findings.matters: The C3 rating represents formal finding of serious service failure affecting 24,000 homes and 53,000 residents. This creates material risk of tenant litigation, regulatory enforcement action, and significant capital costs for remediation. Recovery will require sustained investment and management attention.
findings.figures: C3 regulatory rating assigned 15 January 2025; 24,000 rented homes; 53,000 residents; 2,000+ damp and mould cases outstanding; 16 identified breaches of RSH regulations
findings.quote: The judgement was that this was a grading of C3, this means it is the Regulators assessment that there are serious failings in the landlord delivering the outcomes of the consumer standards and significant improvement is needed.

findings.paper_title: 9.2.1 Appendix A 25 NCC Auditor's Annual Report FINAL
findings.headline: £62.7 million three-year budget gap with £41.5 million of required savings not yet identified beyond 2025/26.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan shows a cumulative funding gap of £62.7 million to 2027/28. The council has identified £21.3 million of savings for 2025/26 but has no detailed proposals for closing the remaining £41.5 million gap in 2026/27 and 2027/28. The council cites 'lack of clarity over future funding' and challenges of 'short-term, single year funding settlements'. While the council holds £247.7 million usable reserves and has £300 million borrowing headroom, two-thirds of required savings remain unspecified.
findings.matters: A lender needs visibility on how a council will maintain financial balance. With £41.5 million still unidentified, there is material risk the council will need to draw reserves faster than planned, increase borrowing beyond forecasts, or implement unplanned service reductions.
findings.figures: £62.7 million cumulative gap by 2027/28; £21.3 million savings identified for 2025/26; £41.5 million unidentified for 2026/27-2027/28; £247.7 million usable reserves; £300 million borrowing headroom
findings.quote: As a result, proposals have not been established for how the Council close the remaining budget gap of £41.5 million in the MTFP (£62.3 million for the period 2025-28).

findings.paper_title: 9.2.1 Appendix A 25 NCC Auditor's Annual Report FINAL
findings.headline: Auditor unable to verify council's financial position for third consecutive year due to lack of evidence over asset valuations.
findings.detail: Ernst & Young issued a disclaimer of opinion on 26 February 2026, unable to obtain sufficient evidence over valuation of land and buildings, PFI obligations, and HRA expenditure. This is the third consecutive year of disclaimer (also 2022/23 and 2023/24). The auditor expects the earliest unqualified opinion will not be until 2028/29, due to cumulative gaps in assurance over opening balances and comparative periods.
findings.matters: A disclaimer means the council's asset position cannot be independently verified. For a lender considering Newcastle's creditworthiness, this prevents verification of the financial position being reported and limits confidence in the council's ability to meet obligations.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued 26 February 2026; unable to obtain assurance on PPE, PFI, HRA; earliest unqualified opinion expected 2028/29
findings.quote: We therefore issued a disclaimer of opinion on the 2024/25 financial statements on the 26 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: The council explicitly identifies over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure as a financial sustainability risk that could trigger government intervention.
findings.detail: The Financial Sustainability and Resilience risk (RED 12) warns that 'over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure' could lead to 'the Council being subject to intervention by government.' The medium-term financial plan for 2026-27 to 2028-29 was approved in March 2026, but the strategy for addressing budget gaps in 2027-28 and 2028-29 is still being developed (due July 2026 for cabinet consideration).
findings.matters: This is an explicit acknowledgment that reserves are currently being used to bridge permanent structural deficits, which is unsustainable and triggers government intervention thresholds. The timing gap (2027-28 planning delayed to July 2026) suggests limited forward visibility.
findings.figures: MTFP 2026-27 to 2028-29 approved March 2026; MTFP 2027-28 to 2029-30 due for consideration July 2026
findings.quote: Inaccurate financial forecasts, under-achievement of agreed savings and over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure could impact negatively on the council's financial sustainability and resilience and lead to the Council being subject to intervention by government.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care CQC assessment in May 2026 identified service deficiencies; the council states it can manage the risk but reputational risk remains Amber.
findings.detail: The CQC published findings on 28 May 2026 with recommendations. The council has a continuous improvement plan in place addressing four themes: timeliness and simplification, experience of process and support, choice and availability of provision, and evidencing impact. The overall Adult Social Care risk remains RED 12, and whilst the director believes mitigation is in place, reputational risk is rated Amber (not resolved).
findings.matters: A CQC inspection that flags deficiencies carries reputational risk and signals service quality concerns; Amber reputational risk means the issue is not fully contained, which could affect recruitment, partnership arrangements, and public confidence.
findings.figures: CQC assessment published 28 May 2026; Adult Social Care risk: RED 12 (unchanged); Reputational risk: Amber
findings.quote: A robust continuous improvement plan in place which addresses recommendations made by the CQC Assessment published in May 2026.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: PFI contract expiries require additional resourcing and management, with multiple handovers in flight across schools, libraries and street lighting.
findings.detail: Newcastle is managing the expiry of multiple PFI contracts across schools (PFI Phase 1, BSF), libraries, LIFT schemes, and street lighting. The council has had to recruit additional resources to manage these handovers and has established dedicated project boards. The PFI risk remains RED 12 but has a target priority of Amber 8, indicating active mitigation. A PFI Partnerships Manager position was out to recruitment as of the report date.
findings.matters: PFI handbacks create transitional risk and cost — assets transfer back to council ownership, FM contracts end, and lifecycle maintenance funds must be reviewed. The need to recruit extra staff signals this is non-trivial in scale.
findings.figures: Two dedicated Project Boards (Schools PFI/BSF and LIFT/Libraries); PFI risk priority: RED 12 to Amber 8 (target); PFI Partnerships Manager position out to recruitment
findings.quote: Project Team with additional resource being recruited

findings.headline: Asset stock condition surveys reveal maintenance backlogs requiring future investment, with results due June 2027.
findings.detail: A housing stock condition survey (HRA) began October 2024 and is expected to complete June 2027. A Public Buildings Condition Survey has already completed and identified a backlog maintenance position and future investment needs. These surveys are being used to inform asset strategy and investment planning, suggesting significant remedial work is known to be ahead.
findings.matters: Completed backlog surveys point to substantial unquantified future capital requirements for building maintenance and safety compliance, which will compete for borrowing headroom and affect financial sustainability planning.
findings.figures: Survey period: October 2024 to June 2027; Public Buildings Condition Survey completed
findings.quote: A Stock condition survey (SCS) and asset strategy is required to give accurate understanding of our stock condition and the investment required to keep it safe and decent. Stock condition survey started October 2024 and expected to be completed by June 2027.

findings.paper_title: 6.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: SEND capital funding does not resolve the underlying revenue and demand pressures driving deficits in the high needs block.
findings.detail: Newcastle has been allocated £2.4m for SEND system reform and capital funding is available (£860m nationally for High Needs places), but the council explicitly states this capital does not address revenue pressures. Independent placements remain costly, specialist school capacity is insufficient, and home-to-school transport costs remain high. The financial assessment of the SEND risk is rated RED 16 (Critical impact), the highest rating in the register.
findings.matters: This reveals a structural mismatch: capital is being deployed where revenue pressures dominate, meaning the council faces ongoing deficits in this service line that cannot be resolved by the funding streams available.
findings.figures: £2.4m allocation to Newcastle; £860m national High Needs Capital allocation for 2026/27; SEND financial assessment: RED 16
findings.quote: The £2.4m investment Newcastle has been allocated supports our sufficiency and inclusion strategy, but on its own does not resolve underlying demand and cost pressures, particularly in high-cost placements and statutory services.

findings.headline: External auditors identified issues regarding assessment of the control environment in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council's external auditors issued their Audit Results Report on the external audit for the year ended 31 March 2025, highlighting issues regarding the control environment. These span financial reporting, asset valuation, record retention, and reconciliation procedures across multiple areas including IFRS 16 compliance, property valuations, and grant income recognition.
findings.matters: Control environment weaknesses identified by external audit indicate potential gaps in financial statement accuracy and internal controls that would concern lenders assessing the council's creditworthiness and financial reporting reliability.
findings.figures: Seven distinct areas of control improvement identified across accounting, reconciliations, valuations, and financial reporting
