findings.headline: Waste disposal cost pressure from Emissions Trading Scheme estimated for 2028-29 but magnitude unknown
findings.detail: The UK government plans to include waste incineration in the Emissions Trading Scheme from 2028, requiring operators to pay for carbon emissions. The council has 'factored in an estimated cost pressure in 2028-29' but the quantum is not specified in this document. The government's 'detailed design and mitigation measures remain under development.'
findings.matters: This is a new regulatory cost arriving with short notice and uncertain magnitude. It will hit all councils simultaneously, reducing flexibility in the waste market.
findings.figures: ETS implementation 2028; two-year monitoring period before scheme comes into effect; cost pressure estimated but not quantified
findings.quote: We have also factored in an estimated cost pressure in 2028-29 in relation to the Emissions Trading Scheme

findings.headline: Outer West Leisure and highway improvements financed by prudential borrowing funded through unidentified 'corporate savings'
findings.detail: The council plans to finance the Outer West Leisure project and additional highway/pavement improvements through prudential borrowing 'funded corporately through savings elsewhere in the budget.' These savings have not been identified. This is circular reasoning: the council is committing to borrow and service the debt from savings it has not yet found to deliver a £81.7m gap.
findings.matters: This suggests the council is committing to capital projects before identifying how to fund them. If the corporate savings do not materialise, the council will need to find funding from cuts to services, or the projects will not proceed.
findings.figures: Borrowing for Outer West Leisure and highways; corporate savings source unspecified; total capital programme ~£160m per annum

findings.headline: HRA stock condition survey not complete until June 2027, limiting ability to forecast major maintenance investment
findings.detail: The council took transfer of the Housing Revenue Account in 2024 and commissioned a 100% stock condition survey starting October 2024. The survey is not expected to be complete until June 2027. Until then, the council does not have accurate data on the investment required to maintain stock to a safe and decent standard. The HRA operates on a self-financing basis and must fund all investment from rents and service charges.
findings.matters: The council cannot produce a reliable 30-year HRA business plan until it knows the actual condition of its stock. This creates uncertainty over future rent levels and the sustainability of HRA finances.
findings.figures: Stock survey started October 2024; expected completion June 2027; HRA budget ~£140m per annum; 100% stock survey commissioned
findings.quote: The stock condition survey started in October 2024 and is expected to be completed by June 2027

findings.headline: Property portfolio under review with unspecified recovery plans for assets generating £3.9m annual overspend
findings.detail: The council's property portfolio overspent by £3.864m in 2025-26. The MTFS states this is due to 'a small number of assets, which are the subject of review and recovery plans.' No details are given of which assets, their current status, or the nature of the recovery plans. This suggests either disposal, major refurbishment, or restructuring of leasing arrangements.
findings.matters: Unspecified asset problems and recovery plans create uncertainty. A lender would want to know which assets are problematic and what the recovery plan entails (e.g., forced sales in a weak market, or investments requiring capital).
findings.figures: £3.864m overspend in 2025-26 from property portfolio
findings.quote: The pressures on the Property Portfolio relate mainly to a small number of assets, which are the subject of review and recovery plans

findings.headline: Adult social care overspent by £5.9m in 2025-26; commissioned care market faces wage and cost pressures
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £5.897m in 2025-26, driven by nursing/residential care and learning difficulty services. The council commissions much of this spend from external providers. The sector faces sustained pressure from National Living Wage increases (now £12.71 per hour), Employers National Insurance contributions, and providers reporting they are 'running some services at a loss' due to low local authority rates. The council has adopted the Real Living Wage (£13.45 per hour) as a requirement for contractors.
findings.matters: Adult social care is forecast to be a growing proportion of council budgets nationally. Cost control is limited when the council is a price-taker in a competitive market and has already imposed minimum wage floors.
findings.figures: £5.897m overspend in 2025-26; National Living Wage £12.71/hour; Real Living Wage £13.45/hour; sector wide adult care costs over £20bn nationally
findings.quote: Within this reported position there were pressures in the...Adult Social Care and Prevention directorate of £5.897 million

findings.headline: Children's social care overspent by £8.3m in 2025-26; national demand grew 20% since 2014
findings.detail: The council's Children's and Families directorate overspent by £8.317m in 2025-26, driven by external residential care, external fostering, and in-house residential staffing costs. Nationally, the number of children in care has risen 20% since 2014. Despite being budgeted for, the overspend recurred, suggesting the budget assumptions underestimate the true cost of delivering the service.
findings.matters: This is a growing statutory service where demand is outpacing funding and cost control. The overspend recurrence suggests forecasting accuracy is poor or costs are genuinely uncontrollable.
findings.figures: £8.317m overspend in 2025-26; 20% increase in children in care nationally since 2014; 83,630 children in care nationally at 2024
findings.quote: Within this reported position there were pressures in the Children's and Families Directorate of £8.317 million

findings.headline: SEND statutory override expires March 2028; remaining deficit will revert to general fund if government does not fund it
findings.detail: The council's High Needs Block deficit is currently ring-fenced under a statutory override, with 90% of the accumulated deficit at March 2026 met by government grant. However, 10% of that deficit plus ongoing deficits in 2027-28 and 2028-29 are not guaranteed funding. When the override expires in March 2028, 'the remaining deficit at this date will be charged to the general fund if insufficient funding is provided from government.' The council has drafted a SEND reform plan but flagged that 'the majority of local authorities are not confident they can continue to meet statutory duties and fund the transition within their current level of funding.'
findings.matters: This is a potential unfunded liability that could hit the general fund in 2028-29. The council has a statutory duty to provide SEND support and cannot refuse this spending, meaning the deficit becomes mandatory budget pressure.
findings.figures: 90% of March 2026 deficit funded by government; 10% plus future deficits not guaranteed; statutory override ends March 2028
findings.quote: The remaining deficit at this date will be charged to the general fund if insufficient funding is provided from government

findings.headline: Relative Needs Assessment methodology shift reduced Newcastle's funding entitlement by 3.6% due to housing cost inclusion
findings.detail: The Fair Funding 2.0 review reassessed funding entitlements using updated deprivation indices that now include housing costs. This shift increased funding for London (due to higher housing costs in the capital) but reduced Newcastle's allocation by 3.6% overall, despite Newcastle being a high-deprivation authority. This represents a permanent reduction in the council's relative share of the funding pot.
findings.matters: This is a structural loss of funding based on government's new assessment of the council's needs. It is not reversible and reflects a shift in policy that disadvantages high-deprivation post-industrial areas.
findings.figures: 3.6% reduction in overall needs assessment; shift of funding towards London
findings.quote: The main reason for this change related to the use of the updated deprivation indices, which now include housing costs. This change has resulted in a significant shift of funding towards London

findings.headline: 2025-26 balance of £0.483m achieved only through £7.2m extraordinary airport dividend; underlying position was £6.7m overspend
findings.detail: The council reported a small general fund underspend of £0.483m in 2025-26, but this masks significant operational overspends. Children's and Families overspent by £8.317m, Adult Social Care by £5.897m, and the Property Portfolio by £3.864m. Without a one-off airport dividend payment of £7.216m, the outturn would have been an overspend of £6.733m. This signals the underlying budget is out of control.
findings.matters: A council relying on one-off windfalls to balance its budget is vulnerable to the next unexpected cost shock. These are core services that are chronically overspending despite being budgeted for inflationary increases.
findings.figures: £8.317m Children's overspend; £5.897m Adult Social Care overspend; £3.864m Property Portfolio overspend; £7.216m extraordinary airport dividend; £6.733m underlying overspend without dividend
findings.quote: Without this payment, the outturn position would have been an overspend of £6.733 million

findings.headline: £81.7 million budget gap over three years with structural deficit requiring sustained savings delivery
findings.detail: The council faces a cumulative budget gap of £81.7 million over 2027-28 to 2029-30, with annual savings requirements of £27.5m, £25.3m and £28.9m respectively. This follows £251 million in savings delivered since 2015. The gap is driven by cost pressures of £121m and only partially offset by £46.5m in funding increases. The council states it will not use reserves to close this gap.
findings.matters: A persistent structural deficit of this scale, after a decade of £251m in cuts, suggests the council has exhausted easy efficiency savings and is facing structural underfunding in relation to demand. Repeated failure to deliver savings would trigger a Section 114 notice.
findings.figures: £81.7m total gap; £251m savings delivered 2015-2027; £121m cost pressures against £46.5m funding growth
findings.quote: the total budget gap over the three year MTFS period is £81.7 million

findings.headline: Property Portfolio overspent by £3.864m with three major assets significantly underperforming: Partnership House £1.367m, The Core Building £1.246m, Higham House £0.730m
findings.detail: Three significant council-owned buildings are generating substantially lower returns or higher costs than budgeted. Partnership House was budgeted to generate £0.3m income but cost £1.1m; The Core Building was budgeted at -£0.2m but cost £1.0m. This suggests either the asset valuations were inaccurate or deterioration in property market conditions or asset performance.
findings.matters: The council's property portfolio is a key asset base; material underperformance suggests either assets require remediation, market conditions have deteriorated, or the portfolio is not generating expected returns.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £5.808m driven by High Needs Block, with statutory override expiring March 2028
findings.detail: The DSG reserve is in deficit by £5.8m due to sustained overspending in the High Needs Block (SEND services). High Needs Block overspent by £6.082m this year alone, driven by rising numbers of EHCPs, independent school placements, and specialist provision. The deficit is currently protected by a statutory override that must expire in March 2028, creating a deadline for structural resolution.
findings.matters: This is a £5.8m liability that cannot currently be covered by the council and must be resolved by March 2028; it signals unsustainable SEND cost growth driven by policy (EHCP expansion) rather than efficiency factors.
findings.figures: £5.808m negative DSG reserve balance; £6.082m High Needs Block overspend in year; statutory override expires March 2028
findings.quote: There was an overspend of £6.082 million in the High Needs Block, an underspend in the Schools Block of £0.087 million and an underspend of £0.611 million in the Early Years Block. With the outturn position of £5.381 million this has resulted in a negative reserve balance of £5.808 million on the DSG. Currently, the Council can account for this as an unusable reserve due to a statutory override agreed by MHCLG, therefore not directly impacting the General Fund and overall financial position of the Council. This was due to expire in March 2026, however government has announced an extension to March 2028.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care Community Support overspent by £8.954m in nursing and residential care, forced into emergency external placements by bed closures
findings.detail: The largest directorate overspend is driven by demand for complex, expensive care: nursing home placements, residential care, and home care for older people and learning disability clients with complex needs (particularly dementia support). Closure of Eden Court and temporary bed reductions at Connie Lewcock have forced the council to use emergency external placements at higher cost.
findings.matters: This reflects structural demographic pressures (aging population, increasing complexity) that are forcing the council into external care provision and reducing capacity to manage costs.
findings.figures: £8.954m overspend in Community Support; nursing care, residential care and home care cited as main drivers
findings.quote: Community Support, which has an overspend of £8.954 million due mainly to demand in relation to older people and learning disability commissioned services. The increase in budget pressure is mainly within nursing care, residential care and home care, with an increase in clients needing more complex and costly dementia support packages. Pressure in the system with the closure of Eden Court and temporary reduction in beds at Connie Lewcock has resulted in increased use of externally commissioned temporary and emergency residential placements and other support.

findings.headline: Children's Social Care overspent by £7.572m with escalating external placement costs and additional placements added in Q4
findings.detail: Children's Social Care is driving major cost pressures through external fostering and residential placements, which cost more than in-house provision. The paper notes additional placements were added in Q4 beyond what was forecast, and staffing costs for in-house services are also rising.
findings.matters: This reflects structural growth in demand for vulnerable children's services with a shift toward expensive external placements; costs are escalating faster than budget provision.
findings.figures: £7.572m overspend in Children's Social Care
findings.quote: Children's Social Care, which has an overspend of £7.572 million due mainly to increased costs of providing services to children in care, especially external fostering placements, external residential placements, children with disabilities and increased costs of staffing of in-house residential services. There have been additional placements since quarter 3.

findings.headline: The £0.483m underspend masks a £6.733m underlying overspend after removing the extraordinary £7.216m airport dividend
findings.detail: The council's headline outturn appears healthy, but entirely depends on a one-off special dividend from its airport investment. Without this extraordinary payment, Newcastle would have overspent by £6.7m. This reveals structural budget pressures beneath the surface.
findings.matters: One-off income cannot fund ongoing commitments; this suggests recurring budget gaps in future years without continued extraordinary income.
findings.figures: £0.483m underspend (headline) vs £6.733m underlying overspend; airport dividend £7.216m
findings.quote: The Council received an extraordinary airport dividend payment of £7.216 million. Without this payment, the outturn position would be an overspend of £6.733 million.

findings.detail: Capital expenditure drops materially in 2026-27 and then flatlines at £80m. The document attributes prior slippage to COVID, construction inflation, and material sourcing problems but does not explain whether the 2026-27 reduction is planned consolidation or reflects ongoing delivery constraints.
findings.matters: A sustained reduction in capital investment, especially on a council with acknowledged maintenance backlogs, raises questions about the council's ability to maintain asset condition and estate quality.
findings.quote: our approved capital expenditure is £105.3 million in 2025-26, £83.8 million in 2026-27, £80.0 million in 2027-28 and £80.0 million in 2028-29 within our General Fund capital programme

findings.headline: Long-term net borrowing of £560.6m expected by March 2027 with sustained capital borrowing of £30m annually through 2028-29
findings.detail: The liability benchmark shows net loans requirement rising from £532.7m to £560.6m by 31 March 2027. The council's long-term forecast assumes capital expenditure funded by borrowing of £30m per year through 2028-29, establishing Newcastle as a sustained net borrower dependent on debt markets for at least three years.
findings.matters: Sustained high net borrowing with capital-dependent growth means the council remains exposed to market conditions; refinancing needs concentrate in periods of elevated rates
findings.figures: Net loans requirement: £532.7m (31.3.25) to £560.6m (31.3.27); assumed capital borrowing £30m/year to 2028-29
findings.quote: Following on from the medium-term forecasts in the table above, the long-term liability benchmark assumes capital expenditure funded by borrowing of £30 million a year to 2028-29.

findings.headline: Rising SEND deficits identified as a cash flow risk that could force early short-term borrowing and increase costs
findings.detail: The strategy explicitly flags that 'increasing SEND deficits could lead to reductions in available cash and therefore lead to short-term borrowing sooner than anticipated.' The council notes this would simultaneously reduce investment interest income while adding additional interest costs on short-term debt, a dual pressure on finances.
findings.matters: SEND deficits are a known sector stress; Newcastle has identified it as capable of forcing unplanned short-term borrowing, suggesting either tight cash position or escalating SEND pressures requiring early intervention
findings.figures: No deficit figure quantified in this section
findings.quote: there is a risk that increasing SEND deficits could lead to reductions in available cash and therefore lead to short-term borrowing sooner than anticipated to fund expected capital expenditure. Should this happen, this would also lead to reductions in investment interest as well as additional interest costs on this short-term borrowing.

findings.headline: £81 million of LOBO loans with options maturing in next 18 months face refinancing at elevated rates
findings.detail: Newcastle holds £141m of LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) loans where lenders can force rate increases on set dates. The council explicitly identifies that £23m have options before 31 March 2026 and £58m more during 2026-27, and notes 'there is still a reasonable chance that lenders will exercise their options' given current elevated interest rates. If called, the council will repay rather than accept higher rates, forcing refinancing of this material amount within the next 18 months.
findings.matters: Refinancing £81m in rapid succession within elevated rate environment creates concentration risk and could force higher interest costs or constrain liquidity; cumulative with other borrowing needs
findings.figures: £141m total LOBO loans; £27m called in 2025-26 and repaid; £23m options before 31 March 2026; £58m options during 2026-27
findings.quote: With interest rates remaining elevated, there is still a reasonable chance that lenders will exercise their options. If they do, we will take the option to repay LOBO loans to reduce refinancing risk in later years.

findings.headline: Interest payable burden flagged as comparatively high; external debt £612m and rising with significant PFI component
findings.detail: CIPFA's financial resilience index identifies Newcastle's interest payable as a proportion of net revenue expenditure as "comparatively high" due to high external debt. The council holds £612m in external loans at end of 2025-26 (against an authorised limit of £911m), and this figure includes notional PFI debt. Nearly half of actual external debt relates to the HRA. The council is currently using internal funds rather than external borrowing, but this is not sustainable long-term.
findings.matters: High interest costs reduce financial flexibility and increase vulnerability to interest rate movements. The fact the council is using internal reserves to avoid external borrowing suggests the cost of new external debt is now material.
findings.figures: External debt £612m; authorised limit £911m; PFI component ~half of actual external debt
findings.quote: Interest payable as a proportion of net revenue expenditure – the council's level of spend on interest payable as a proportion of net revenue expenditure is comparatively high. This is due to the comparatively high level of debt... estimated level of external loans at the end of the 2025-26 financial year is £612.0 million, compared to an authorised limit of £911.2 million.

findings.headline: HRA reserves depleted to £3.4m by end of 2025-26; ongoing Right to Buy losses and stock condition survey risks threaten 30-year viability
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account reserves have been eroded from historical levels to just £3.4m by March 2026 due to past rent freezes and rising damp/mould and repair costs. The council is undertaking stock condition surveys with potential to further increase repairs budget pressure. Right to Buy sales continue to reduce stock, though amendments to the scheme are proposed nationally.
findings.matters: The HRA is ring-fenced but held by the same council. Unsustainable HRA finances force difficult choices on rents, investment, or cross-subsidy from the general fund. A critically low reserve leaves no buffer for structural repairs or compliance costs.
findings.figures: HRA reserves £3.4m at March 2026
findings.quote: HRA reserves are projected to fall to approximately £3.4 million by the end of 2025-26. A combination of the impact of rent freezes in recent years, and increased costs in relation to damp and mould and repairs, has eroded the level of HRA reserves and therefore presents a risk within the 30 year business plan.

findings.headline: CFO confirms council not in Section 114 territory but is operating in "extremely challenging financial circumstances" requiring ongoing review
findings.detail: The CFO concludes "the council is not currently in a position where a section 114 notice is required" but immediately adds "It should however be noted that the council is operating within extremely challenging financial circumstances and therefore the position will continue to be reviewed." This is the formal equivalent of saying the council is borderline and under close watch.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice signals a council cannot set a balanced budget and typically precedes intervention. The CFO explicitly flagging ongoing review of this threshold is a material governance alert.
findings.figures: Section 114 assessment ongoing; unprecedented numbers of councils in distress nationally
findings.quote: The budget assumptions set out within this report have been assessed in the light of the Chief Finance Officer's responsibilities under section 114 of the Local Government Finance Act 1988 and his conclusion is that the council is not currently in a position where a section 114 notice is required. It should however be noted that the council is operating within extremely challenging financial circumstances and therefore the position will continue to be reviewed.

findings.headline: £37.4 million capital pipeline unfunded in 2026-27, escalating to £157.3m unfunded in 2027-28 and £167.2m in 2028-29
findings.detail: The council has identified capital projects totalling £37.4m in 2026-27, £157.3m in 2027-28 and £167.2m in 2028-29 with "no funding approved yet." These will require either external borrowing, capital receipts, or grant awards not yet secured. The sudden scale increase from 2027-28 suggests major schemes awaiting approval or funding clarification.
findings.matters: Unsecured capital pipelines indicate future borrowing needs or reliance on grants not yet approved. Both create either an increase in debt servicing costs or planning risk if grants are not forthcoming.
findings.quote: Pipeline (no funding approved yet) 0.0 37.4 157.3 167.2

findings.headline: £55.2 million of specific grant rolled into Revenue Support Grant in 2026-27, creating funding model uncertainty the CFO explicitly flags as difficult to model
findings.detail: The council will absorb £55.2m of previously-ring-fenced specific grants into the general RSG, with a further £20.8m consolidation from 2027-28. The CFO states "Estimation of the amount due in government funding has been difficult to model this year due to these changes" and notes the hybrid approach "potentially increases the longer term uncertainty in the system." While spending commitments are meant to transfer with the grant, the loss of ring-fencing reduces certainty.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on stable, predictable revenue streams. Major changes to the composition of funding, especially moving from specific to general grants, introduce uncertainty about the council's ability to deliver committed services.
findings.figures: £55.2m rolled into RSG 2026-27; £20.8m further from 2027-28; total change £76.0m
findings.quote: An increase of £64.1 million in the amount of Revenue Support Grant income receivable. This includes £55.2 million of former specific grant funding that has now been rolled into the RSG as outlined in the provisional local government finance settlement... Estimation of the amount due in government funding has been difficult to model this year due to these changes.

findings.headline: Adult and children's social care overspends of £8.9m driven by demand not yet addressed by change programme
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is £3.9m over budget at Q2 due to higher demand in learning disability, physical disability and older people services. Children's Social Care is £5.0m over at Q2, primarily from increased costs of external residential and fostering placements. Combined, these represent 1.8% of total budget spend and are demand-driven pressures the council identifies but whose resolution is not explicitly detailed.
findings.matters: Social care is typically the largest and least flexible budget area for councils. Demand-driven overspends signal demographic or system pressures beyond the council's control, and are historically sticky items.
findings.figures: Adult Social Care overspend £3.9m; Children's Social Care overspend £5.0m (both Q2 2025-26); combined £8.9m
findings.quote: Adult Social Care and Prevention (projected overspend of £3.9 million at Q2) due mainly to higher than expected demand in relation to demand in learning disability, physical disability and older people commissioned services. Children's Social Care (projected overspend of £5.0 million at Q2) due mainly to increased costs of providing services to children in care, especially external residential and fostering placements.

findings.headline: General fund unearmarked reserve will fall to £8.5 million if 2025-26 overspend materialises, below the council's assessed £18.4 million adequacy level
findings.detail: The council currently holds an unearmarked reserve of £18.1m. A projected £9.6m overspend in 2025-26 would reduce this to £8.5m (down from £18.4m assessed as adequate). The council explicitly states it "will need to develop options to increase the level of the unearmarked General Fund reserve back up to £18.4 million as part of the 2025-26 outturn." This means no buffer is currently available for unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Reserves are the last line of defence for a council's financial stability. Falling significantly below adequacy levels while facing multiple unfunded pressures limits the council's ability to absorb shocks.
findings.figures: Current unearmarked reserve £18.1m; projected end 2025-26 £8.5m; assessed adequate level £18.4m; Q2 overspend risk £9.6m
findings.quote: If this is the position at the end of the financial year then this pressure would need to be funded from the unearmarked General Fund reserve thus potentially reducing the balance from £18.1 million to £8.5 million as at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: DSG deficit will reach £18 million by end of 2027-28, creating sustained reserve pressure with no clarity on post-override treatment
findings.detail: The council's accumulated Dedicated Schools Grant deficit is projected to rise from £0.4m at March 2025 to £7.8m by March 2026, and £18m by end of 2027-28. While government will cover 90% of eligible deficits at March 2026, the treatment of the remaining 10% and future deficits is unresolved. Once fully accumulated, this will cost the council approximately £0.6m annually in lost investment returns. The statutory override expires March 2028; the SEND White Paper expected to clarify treatment has been delayed until early 2026.
findings.matters: DSG deficits are ringfenced and cannot be merged with general reserves, but the council still holds the cash shortfall, creating a material annual opportunity cost and constraining financial flexibility at a critical moment.
findings.figures: DSG deficit £7.8m at March 2026; £18m at end of 2027-28; £0.6m annual opportunity cost at 3.5% investment return
findings.quote: The cumulative deficit at the end of 2027-28 is now projected at £18 million, following the announcement of grant funding. This level of ringfenced cumulative deficit would place an annual pressure of approximately £0.6 million on the General Fund.

findings.headline: Non-domestic rates appeals provision overstated by £9.0 million; corrected after delayed data update
findings.detail: Council maintained overstated provision based on outdated claims data. Updated Analyse Local platform data showed significantly lower requirement. Corrected downward by £9.0m. Shows reactive rather than timely data management.
findings.matters: Indicates reserves quality depends on timely access to external data; potential provisioning delays affect accuracy of financial position
findings.figures: £9.0 million
findings.quote: This resulted in a reduction of £9.0 million as detailed in section 05 of this report, and we concluded that the adjustments made were accurate and appropriate

findings.headline: £8.7 million share of pension fund asset valuation variance indicates uncertainty in major liability
findings.detail: Tyne and Wear Pension Fund auditor identified £52.5m discrepancy between investment assets submitted to actuary versus fund manager confirmations. Newcastle's apportioned share is £8.7 million. Auditors included as judgemental misstatement but assessed impact as not material.
findings.matters: Pension liability is material balance; asset valuation discrepancy creates uncertainty about true funding position and council contribution requirements
findings.figures: £52.5 million (total fund), £8.7 million (council apportionment)
findings.quote: We obtained assurances from the auditor of the Tyne and Wear Pension Fund who reported a difference in the total value of investment assets submitted to the actuary against the value of investments per the confirmations from the fund managers, amounting to £52.5 million for the total fund. We apportioned this difference to calculate the Council's share of the misstatement, which was £8.7 million

findings.headline: Fraudulent overtime claims investigation not initially disclosed in Annual Governance Statement
findings.detail: Audit identified fraud investigation at council relating to fraudulent overtime claims within a specific function. This was not disclosed in AGS; auditors raised with management and AGS update was agreed but not yet confirmed received.
findings.matters: Shows initial governance reporting weakness and indicates control environment issues within payroll/HR systems
findings.figures: No amount disclosed
findings.quote: We identified that this did not disclose a fraud investigation that had taken place at the Council relating to fraudulent overtime claims within a specific function. This was raised with management, and it was agreed that the Annual Governance Statement would be updated to reflect these findings

findings.headline: Auditors seeking unquantified scale fee variation for additional work due to incomplete audit procedures and poor working paper quality
findings.detail: Multiple references to scale fee variation expected due to: inability to complete PPE procedures; significant delays in receipt of working papers across leases, PFI, PPE, debtors, creditors; poor quality of supporting evidence; substantial delays from property team requiring extension beyond planned audit window.
findings.matters: Indicates additional cost burden to council; reflects audit resource inefficiency driven by control weaknesses and documentation deficiencies
findings.figures: Magnitude not quantified in draft report
findings.quote: We expect to raise a scale fee variation to reflect the work performed and considerable additional time spent on leases, PFI, and PPE including componentisation

findings.headline: £14.3 million of grant and Community Infrastructure Levy income recognition errors in section 106 and CIL balances
findings.detail: £7.2m overstatement of CIL income received in advance (inappropriate recognition despite no repayment conditions); £4.7m understatement of section 106 grants received in advance; £2.4m understatement of other income received in advance. Corrected via reconciliation.
findings.matters: Indicates controls weakness over conditional vs unconditional income recognition; impacts both reported income and deferred income liabilities
findings.figures: £7.2 million overstatement CIL; £4.7 million understatement s106 grants; £2.4 million understatement other income
findings.quote: £7.2 million overstatement of grant income received in advance due to the inappropriate recognition as grants received in advance for Community Infrastructure Levy (CIL) income where there are no repayment conditions, and a £4.7 million understatement of grants received in advance and £2.4 million understatement of income received in advance relating to s106 balances

findings.headline: Multiple long-term debtor errors totalling £14.8 million indicating weak debtor management controls
findings.detail: Series of errors: £2.5m loan not finalised before year-end incorrectly included in statements; £3.7m receivable within 12 months misclassified as long-term; £6.5m YHN loan not removed after repayment; £2.1m classification misstatement between short and long-term.
findings.matters: Pattern of errors reflects weak receivables controls; impacts both balance sheet accuracy and visibility of actual cash inflows
findings.figures: £2.5 million + £3.7 million + £6.5 million + £2.1 million
findings.quote: Loan of £2.5 million was not finalised before 31 March 2025 and is incorrect to include in the financial statements. Loan of £3.7 million was receivable within 12 months and should have been included as a short-term debtor. £6.5 million loan to YHN had not been removed from the long-term debtors note after being repaid.

findings.headline: Material IFRS 16 lease implementation errors with £38.9 million understatement of lease liabilities identified
findings.detail: High-level errors in lease accounting predominantly caused by failure to consider rent reviews in calculations. Identified £38.9 million understatement of future minimum lease payments receivable and £31.0 million understatement of total undisclosed lease liabilities.
findings.matters: Shows systematic accounting control weakness in major asset class; suggests liabilities may be understated across multiple areas
findings.figures: Understatement of future minimum lease payments receivable £38.9 million; Understatement of undiscounted lease liabilities £31.0 million
findings.quote: Understatement of future minimum lease payments receivable of £38.9 million. Understatement of total undiscounted lease liabilities of £31.0 million.

findings.headline: £197.4 million of land and buildings valuations unaudited due to loss of property team staff
findings.detail: Unable to complete audit procedures on PPE held at Existing Use Value/Fair Value after loss of key property valuer. Council unable to provide satisfactory evidence within audit timeframe. Outstanding componentisation issue from 2023/24 remains uncorrected in draft accounts.
findings.matters: Major asset class unverified; suggests systematic valuation control weakness; componentisation error indicates assets may be significantly misstated
findings.figures: Land and Buildings held at EUV/FV - £197.4 million
findings.quote: We were unable to complete our audit procedures relating to the valuation of PPE as management were unable to provide satisfactory responses to our audit queries within the scheduled audit timeframe

findings.headline: Auditors planning to disclaim opinion on 2024/25 financial statements, second year in succession
findings.detail: Unable to obtain sufficient evidence over in-year movements and closing balances. Despite completing in-year transaction testing, lack of assurance over opening balances from disclaimed 2023/24 opinion means auditors cannot conclude 2024/25 statements are free from material misstatement.
findings.matters: Financial statements are unaudited; lenders cannot rely on certified accounts to assess council's financial position
findings.figures: Disclaimer expected similar to 2023/24
findings.quote: we are unable to conclude that the 2024/25 financial statements are free from material and pervasive misstatement of the financial statements. We therefore anticipate issuing a disclaimed 2024/25 audit opinion

findings.paper_title: 5.13 Appendix 13 Minimum Revenue Provision Policy Statement
findings.headline: Newcastle is making £10.2m in voluntary debt overpayments across 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.detail: The council is applying Voluntary Revenue Provision (VRP) of £5.2m in 2025-26 and £5.0m in 2026-27, charging more debt repayment to the revenue budget than the statutory minimum requires. VRP can be reclaimed in later years if the council deems it necessary or prudent.
findings.matters: This represents a material voluntary charge against revenue (£10.2m over two years) and shows how Newcastle is managing its debt strategy and balance sheet capacity.
findings.figures: VRP 2025-26: £5.2m; VRP 2026-27: £5.0m; Total estimated VRP: £10.2m
findings.quote: VRP estimated to be charged in 2025-26 is  £5.2m VRP estimated to be charged in 2026-27 is  £5.0m Total estimated VRP            £10.2m

findings.headline: Section 114 notice not currently required but council explicitly flagging it remains a risk if circumstances worsen
findings.detail: The CFO states 'the council is not currently in a position where a section 114 notice is required' but immediately adds 'It should however be noted that the council is operating within extremely challenging financial circumstances and therefore the position will continue to be reviewed.' This is a material caveat. The council is on the edge of the threshold.
findings.matters: A Section 114 notice is a formal declaration that a council cannot afford its spending and must pause commitments. The fact that the CFO is mentioning it as a live risk (not a theoretical one) is significant.
findings.figures: Unearmarked reserve may fall to £8.5m (vs. £18.4m required); Q2 overspend £9.6m
findings.quote: It should however be noted that the council is operating within extremely challenging financial circumstances and therefore the position will continue to be reviewed.

findings.headline: Capital programme has £126.6m–£130.0m funding pipeline with no approval yet for 2027-28 and 2028-29
findings.detail: The capital programme shows planned investment of £130m in 2027-28 and 2028-29, but Table 8 shows 'Pipeline (no funding approved yet)' at £126.6m and £130.0m for those years respectively. This means the council is planning a capital programme without secured funding. While this is not uncommon (councils do plan ahead), it means significant uncertainty about what will actually be built and when borrowing will be needed.
findings.matters: A capital programme is only credible if it is funded. Unbudgeted capital spend drives unbudgeted borrowing and revenue costs (debt service). A lender will want to know how this will be financed.
findings.figures: 2027-28 capital programme £130m, of which £126.6m is pipeline with no funding; 2028-29 capital programme £130m, of which £130.0m is pipeline with no funding
findings.quote: Table 8 – planned capital investment by source of finance ... Pipeline (no funding approved yet) 0.0 10.1 126.6 130.0

findings.headline: SEND placement costs driven by lack of local specialist school capacity, forcing use of expensive independent provision
findings.detail: The high-needs DSG overspend is primarily driven by increasing numbers of children assessed as needing an EHCP and the council's inability to place them in local specialist schools. The council has limited specialist school places (particularly for autism and complex needs) so children are either placed in more expensive independent/non-maintained special schools outside the city or held in interim arrangements. The council has added 119 specialist school places since 2021 but demand is outpacing supply. This is a structural mismatch, not just a spending control issue.
findings.matters: Rising SEND costs are a national problem but Newcastle's local capacity shortage means it is paying premium rates for scarce provision. Until local capacity matches demand, the cost pressure will persist.
findings.figures: DSG High Needs Block overspend £7.4m (2025-26 Q2 forecast); 119 new specialist places added since 2021; increasing number of EHCPs; use of higher-cost INMSS provision
findings.quote: Increasing numbers of parents whose children have an EHCP are also choosing a specialist learning provider (Specialist School) for their child. We have a limited number of Specialist School places available, particularly for those with complex needs and those requiring autism-specific support. As a result, some children have had to access higher cost Independent and Non Maintained Special School (INMSS) provision outside the city

findings.headline: Business rates reset and 2026 revaluation create material uncertainty in revenue forecast
findings.detail: The business rates system is being reset (first time in years) and there is a 2026 revaluation of ratable values underway. The CFO acknowledges 'increased degree of uncertainty' because multipliers may not adjust neutrally to the revaluation, and the Autumn Budget introduced new multipliers that complicate the scheme further. Newcastle's own business rates base is assumed flat (zero growth) in the forecast. The provisional settlement won't arrive until late December 2025, meaning the budget is built on estimates that will need revision.
findings.matters: A large percentage of the budget (£113.6m in 2026-27) depends on business rates, but the council does not know with confidence what the system will deliver. If actual rates prove lower, the council has a budget gap with no time to adjust.
findings.figures: Business rates income in 2026-27: £113.6m (incl. grants); business rates base growth assumed at 0%; business rates multiplier increase assumed at 3.8%
findings.quote: The business rates system is due to be reset and this was confirmed in the Autumn Budget. We will be informed of our draft allocation in the Provisional Local Government Finance Settlement in late December and we will therefore need to update our assumptions in the draft budget once these figures are available.

findings.headline: Debt servicing cost is 18.7% of core spending power, well above English median
findings.detail: Newcastle's debt servicing (interest and principal repayment) consumes 18.7% of core spending power against a median of lower across England. This is above both the CIPFA nearest neighbours median and all English authorities. Total external debt is £612m. While the council is well within its prudential borrowing limit (£612m actual vs £911m authorized), the debt service burden is constrained relative to peers. This leaves less room for new borrowing or unexpected costs.
findings.matters: High debt servicing as a proportion of spending power is a leading indicator of financial stress and limits the council's ability to respond to shocks or fund new investment.
findings.figures: External loans £612.0m; authorized limit £911.2m; debt servicing 18.7% of core spending power; total debt 304.5% of core spending power
findings.quote: Debt servicing as percentage of core spending power – the council's figure of 18.7% is above the statistical median for both the CIPFA Nearest Neighbours and all English local authorities.

findings.headline: Savings targets escalating from £3.9m (2026-27) to £19.8m (2027-28) as cost pressures persist
findings.detail: The council must find £3.9m in savings for 2026-27, delivered by a 75-FTE staffing reduction and transformation programme. But the underlying cost pressures are not going away: pay inflation, SEND demand, social care demand. By 2027-28, the savings requirement quintuples to £19.8m, suggesting either the cost pressures will worsen or the transformation will need to deliver much deeper cuts.
findings.matters: Escalating savings targets are a warning sign that the council has not solved the underlying problem. A pattern of growing annual targets often precedes a council in difficulty.
findings.figures: 2026-27: £3.9m savings needed, 75 FTE reduction (~1% of workforce); 2027-28: £19.8m savings required; 2028-29: £16.4m required
findings.quote: Table 2 – annual budget changes ... Annual savings required (3.9) (19.8) (16.4)

findings.headline: HRA reserves falling to £3.4m (very tight) amid damp, mould and repair cost pressures
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is self-financing from rents. Reserve erosion from past rent freezes, plus rising costs for damp and mould remediation and fire safety compliance, will leave HRA reserves at only £3.4m by end of 2025-26. Stock condition surveys now underway have potential to increase repair budget strain further. Net zero investment will add to capital pressure. This matters because the HRA has limited flexibility — it cannot raid the General Fund.
findings.matters: A self-financing housing account with reserves at this level has little buffer for unexpected costs or to fund the capital investment needed for compliance. The council's ability to address housing disrepair is constrained.
findings.figures: HRA reserves projected at £3.4m by end of 2025-26; HRA budgeted surplus only £0.1m in 2026-27
findings.quote: A combination of the impact of rent freezes in recent years, and increased costs in relation to damp and mould and repairs, has eroded the level of HRA reserves and therefore presents a risk within the 30 year business plan. HRA reserves are projected to fall to approximately £3.4 million by the end of 2025-26.

findings.headline: Current-year overspend of £9.6m at Q2 could drain unearmarked reserves from £18.1m to £8.5m
findings.detail: Multiple services are overspending: Adult Social Care £3.9m, Children's Social Care £5.0m, DSG £7.4m, Transport £1.5m, Legal Services £1.0m, Property portfolio £4.5m pressure. The council's Q2 combined projection is £9.6m overspend. If this materializes, the unearmarked reserve (the council's last line of defence) will fall well below the £18.4m the CFO says is needed to cover identified financial risks. The council will need to find extra money to replenish it in 2025-26.
findings.matters: This shows the council cannot hold its budget even with known pressures accounted for. A reserve falling below the risk-assessed minimum is a material weakness in financial resilience.
findings.figures: Q2 projected overspend £9.6m; unearmarked reserve falling from £18.1m to potentially £8.5m; required minimum £18.4m
findings.quote: At Q2 there is a projected overspend of £9.6 million. If this is the position at the end of the financial year then this pressure would need to be funded from the unearmarked General Fund reserve thus potentially reducing the balance from £18.1 million to £8.5 million as at 31 March 2026.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit growing to £25m by 2028 despite statutory override masking it
findings.detail: The DSG is forecast to overspend by £7.4m in 2025-26, creating a negative reserve that will reach £7.8m by March 2026 and grow to £25m by end of 2027-28. The statutory override hiding this from the usable reserve calculation expires March 2028. Even with proposed government transfer of SEND spending, the cumulative deficit treatment remains uncertain. At 3.5% cost of capital, the £25m deficit will cost the council £0.9m per year in lost investment returns.
findings.matters: This is a structural problem (not a one-off) that will either blow a hole in usable reserves when the override ends or remain off-balance but economically costly. The OBR forecasts this will reach £14bn nationally.
findings.figures: £7.4m overspend in 2025-26; £7.8m deficit by March 2026; £25m projected by March 2028; £0.9m annual opportunity cost at 3.5% return rate
findings.quote: The cumulative deficit at the end of 2027-28 is projected at £25 million. This level of ringfenced cumulative deficit would place an annual pressure of approximately £0.9 million on the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: 11.1 A Annual evaluation of the effectiveness of Audit & Standards Committee
findings.headline: Committee oversight of major capital projects has declined and respondents report it remains an area needing improvement
findings.detail: The committee's score for reviewing major projects to ensure governance arrangements are in place has declined from 4.4 in 2019 to 3.8 in 2025. A respondent explicitly states 'reporting of major projects through to the committee is an area that could be improved', indicating capital schemes may not be receiving adequate scrutiny by the committee.
findings.matters: Major capital projects are where councils typically face greatest financial risks; weak committee oversight of project governance means cost overruns, delays, or governance failures may not be caught early.
findings.quote: Reporting of major projects through to the committee is an area that could be improved.

findings.paper_title: 11.1 A Annual evaluation of the effectiveness of Audit & Standards Committee
findings.headline: Committee's oversight of whether management effectively tracks performance has significantly weakened, falling from 4.8 in 2019 to 3.5 in 2025

findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council's leadership is effectively tracking financial and operational performance; weakening committee oversight of this function suggests potential gaps in management's ability to identify and respond to financial pressures.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Appendix F - Financial Sustainability Risk Deep Dive - Final
findings.headline: Financial sustainability is rated Red 12 (medium likelihood, critical impact), indicating potential government intervention risk.
findings.detail: The risk assessment identifies inaccurate financial forecasting, unrealised savings delivery, and unsustainable reserve draws as key vulnerabilities. Contributing factors include over-ambitious savings targets, lack of a robust medium-term financial plan, ineffective leadership, inadequate governance, weak financial management, and insufficient reserves.
findings.matters: A Red rating with critical impact indicates the council faces risks that could trigger government intervention, representing a material credit concern that directly affects lending decisions.
findings.figures: Red 12 rating (medium likelihood, critical impact); target rating is Amber 9 (low likelihood, critical impact)
findings.quote: Inaccurate financial forecasts, under-achievement of agreed savings, and over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure could impact negatively on the Council's financial sustainability and resilience and lead to the Council being subject to intervention by government.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Appendix F - Financial Sustainability Risk Deep Dive - Final
findings.headline: The council's Dedicated Schools Grant deficit will reach approximately £25 million with statutory override protection ending March 2028 and no clarity on treatment.
findings.detail: Newcastle's DSG deficit is currently covered by statutory override, but this protection expires when SEND responsibility transfers to government in March 2028. The government has not clarified what happens to the accumulated deficit. If the council must charge it to general fund reserves, it would create a significant financial challenge and trigger unprecedented numbers of Section 114 notices across local government.
findings.matters: A £25m liability requiring resolution by March 2028 represents either a future draw on reserves (weakening liquidity) or forced accounting restatement, both material concerns for lenders assessing financial resilience.
findings.figures: Newcastle projected DSG deficit approximately £25 million; OBR estimates accumulated national deficit could reach £14 billion; statutory override expires March 2028
findings.quote: If the statutory override were to end at this date with no solution to the deficit, the balance would need to be recognised within the usable general fund reserves. This would create a significant financial challenge for the majority of councils, and would inevitably lead to an unprecedented number of Section 114 Notices.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Appendix F - Financial Sustainability Risk Deep Dive - Final
findings.headline: Newcastle faces a 3.6% reduction in its relative needs assessment under Fair Funding Reform 2.0, contrary to earlier expectations.
findings.detail: The council initially expected to benefit from the funding reform based on the August 2025 consultation, but the government's Policy Statement released in November 2025 revealed a 3.6% loss. The change results from updated deprivation indices excluding housing costs, shifting funding toward London and away from other areas.
findings.matters: A reduction in the government's formal assessment of funding needs translates directly to lower grant income for future years, worsening revenue position and reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 3.6% loss in relative needs assessment; initial projection was a slight gain
findings.quote: This shows that our previously projected slight gain in relative needs assessment is now a loss of 3.6%. The main reason for this change was due to the updated deprivation indices used in the formula. These now exclude housing costs, which has resulted in a significant shift of funding into London and away from other areas across England.

findings.paper_title: 7.3 Appendix F - Financial Sustainability Risk Deep Dive - Final
findings.headline: The 2025-26 Q2 projected outturn shows a potential pressure of £9.6m, reversing the £0.5m underspend from 2024-25.
findings.detail: The council achieved a balanced position with a £0.5m underspend in 2024-25, but Q2 2025-26 projections show a significant swing to £9.6m pressure. The report emphasises that managers across the council must focus fully on reducing this pressure before year-end.
findings.matters: A swing from underspend to significant pressure in consecutive years indicates deteriorating budget control and suggests the council may struggle to deliver its financial targets, a material concern for lenders.
findings.figures: 2024-25 final outturn: £0.5m underspend; 2025-26 Q2 projected outturn: £9.6m pressure
findings.quote: Although the 2024-25 final outturn was an underspend of £0.5m, the 2025-26 Q2 projected outturn is a potential pressure of £9.6m. As in previous years, managers across the council will need to fully focus on reducing this pressure before the end of the financial year.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: Asset Management Red 12 with structural condition risks across council property estate
findings.detail: Asset Management is rated Red 12 (Medium likelihood, Critical impact), citing failure to manage council land and property effectively, with unknown structural issues and unquantified maintenance defects. Strategic Asset Management Plan was approved March 2025. Public Buildings Condition Survey started 2024 due December 2025. Housing stock condition survey started October 2024 is not due to complete until June 2027.
findings.matters: Unknown building condition represents a hidden liability. findings.paper_title: 7.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: Adult Social Care Red 12 from funding pressures and social care market instability
findings.detail: Adult Social Care is rated Red 12 (High likelihood, Significant impact). Risks include funding pressures, social care market instability (provider viability), and workforce retention. The council is implementing fortnightly budget monitoring with Service Managers and delivering in-year savings through its Efficiency Programme, suggesting active cost containment effort.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a council's largest controllable budget and highly sensitive to demographic and cost-of-care inflation. Market instability (care providers closing or withdrawing) and workforce turnover both push costs up and service quality down. Red 12 with High likelihood suggests budget gaps are structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: Risk rated Red 12 (High likelihood, Significant impact); fortnightly budget monitoring in place; Efficiency Programme savings delivery tracked through Budget Implementation Group
findings.quote: Failure to achieve effective outcomes for service users, exacerbated by funding pressures and the instability of the social care market including workforce and retention issues.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: Children's Social Care remains Red 12 with funding pressures in a statutory, non-negotiable service
findings.detail: Children's Social Care faces Red 12 risk (High likelihood, Significant impact) with funding pressures, service capacity constraints, and workforce pressures. The council cites 'rising poverty', 'more than a decade of austerity', welfare reform, and 'surging costs of living' as compounding factors. A weekly high-cost placement panel monitors placement decisions and expenditure, indicating cost containment is difficult. The May 2025 Ofsted inspection found strong relational practice but did not address financial sustainability.
findings.matters: Children's social care is statutory — quality cannot be cut. When this service is Red 12 with High likelihood, it signals the council is likely experiencing budget overspend that cannot be managed away. Placement costs are demand-driven and volatile. Persistent Red rating here often precedes wider council budget stress and reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Risk rated Red 12 (High likelihood, Significant impact); weekly high-cost placement panel; May 2025 Ofsted inspection completed
findings.quote: Failure to deliver our statutory responsibilities exacerbated by funding pressures and service capacity due to rising poverty, more than a decade of austerity and welfare reform, the COVID-19 pandemic, risks relating to workforce pressures and surging costs of living.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final

findings.detail: Housing Services is rated Red 12 (Medium likelihood, Critical impact). A review of the HRA business model is underway to assess long-term viability. Housing stock condition survey started October 2024 is not due to complete until June 2027. An internal audit of housing governance is scheduled for 2025/26.
findings.matters: Recent governance restructure in April 2025 combined with HRA business model review suggests the council had to intervene in housing management. Long timescale for asset condition assessment (31 months start to finish) implies the council does not yet understand its maintenance backlog or future capital requirements. HRA sustainability is a ring-fenced matter affecting borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: Governance framework implemented April 2025; housing stock condition survey started October 2024, expected completion June 2027; internal audit scheduled 2025/26
findings.quote: Failure to deliver the Council's vision for council housing and its commitments as set out in the Council's Housing Strategy could result in the Council's long-term plans to deliver safe, quality, sustainable housing and services to residents being compromised, with regulatory and financial obligations not being met.

findings.paper_title: 7.1 Strategic and Corporate Risk Monitoring Report - Final
findings.headline: Financial Sustainability rated Red 12 with specific concern about over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure
findings.detail: The council identifies 'Inaccurate financial forecasts, under-achievement of agreed savings and over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure' as a continuing Red 12 risk (High likelihood, Significant impact). This risk is presented as a deep dive item to the Audit Committee. The Medium-Term Financial Plan for 2026-27 to 2028-29 was presented to Cabinet 15 December 2025, but the council states the 'approach to be developed for addressing budget gaps in 2027-28 and 2028-29', meaning two of the three years covered are still unfunded.
findings.matters: Over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent spending is unsustainable. Government intervention doctrine focuses on this exact condition — structural deficits funded by one-off resources. A council unable to balance spending from current income within 3 years becomes a lending risk and potential intervention candidate.
findings.figures: Red 12 risk (High likelihood, Significant impact); MTFP 2026-27 to 2028-29 presented 15 December 2025; approach to 2027-28 and 2028-29 budget gaps 'to be developed'
findings.quote: Inaccurate financial forecasts, under-achievement of agreed savings and over-reliance on reserves to fund permanent expenditure could impact negatively on the council's financial sustainability and resilience and lead to the Council being subject to intervention by government.

findings.matters: SEND overspend demonstrates the council cannot contain costs in a statutory, demand-driven service. High needs placements are expensive and non-discretionary. Current overspend signals either insufficient government funding, service demand growth outpacing budget, or inability to manage placement costs — all of which require reserve drawdown or service reduction.

findings.paper_title: Appendix - Treasury Management Mid Year Update
findings.headline: The council is using internal cash reserves to fund capital expenditure rather than external borrowing, despite having £287 million of unused authorised borrowing capacity
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is using internal funds in place of external borrowing to part-fund capital financing requirements. External borrowing decreased by £29.5m in the first half (from £643.8m to £614.3m), though £27m was due to LOBO calls. The council has significant headroom (£287.1m authorised limit less £815.4m borrowing), but is choosing to deplete cash reserves for capital instead.
findings.matters: This strategic choice preserves external borrowing capacity for contingencies but depletes cash reserves. Given the council started the year with £112.1m (well above the £10m target), this is currently manageable, but the trajectory of cash deployment and capital spending plans needs monitoring.

findings.headline: £141m of LOBO loans could be called for refinancing over the next four years.
findings.detail: Newcastle holds £141m in Lender Option Borrower Option loans that create a contingent refinancing obligation. Lenders can call these to force refinancing at higher rates: £38m could be called by March 2026, £43m in 2026/27, £40m in 2027/28, and £20m in 2028/29. Two LOBO lenders already exercised options in the first half of 2025-26, calling £27m which was repaid without penalty.
findings.matters: LOBO call events represent a material refinancing risk that could significantly increase debt costs if exercises during higher interest rate periods; this affects the council's debt service budget and cash position.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle's SEND transport savings reach £584,000 of £695,000 target; schools-deficit grant covers up to 90%
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle upon Tyne City Council's children's SEND transport workstream has delivered £584,000 in 2026/27 against a target of £695,000, or 84%, according to the change and innovation update before Cabinet on 16 November. SEND means special educational needs and disabilities. The update says the savings came primarily through route optimisation.

The same update says Independent Travel Training will contribute £125,000, including a £25,000 saving in 2026/27 that is on track. The workstream will also deliver the Children and Families contribution to a separate £1.9m target over three years.

The directorate budgets summary says the Department for Education has confirmed that the High Needs Stability Grant will cover up to 90% of the council's dedicated schools grant deficit as at 31 March 2026. The dedicated schools grant is the government grant that funds schools, and high needs is the part for children with special educational needs. The paper says "Future funding arrangements to support the remaining DSG deficit have not yet been confirmed." The statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps such a deficit off the council's main balance sheet, is due to conclude on 31 March 2028.

The revenue and capital plan says no further deficit write-off was announced in the Autumn Budget 2026 and that the Budget provided no new funding for SEND. It reports pressures in the 2026/27 monitoring from more pupils eligible for SEND support and the cost of meeting it.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle ended 2025-26 with a £0.483m underspend against a budget of about £1.2bn
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle City Council finished the 2025-26 financial year with an underspend of £0.483m, according to a performance report going to its Corporate Scrutiny Committee on 8 October. The figure is the outturn, meaning the actual result for the year once it had ended, as against what was budgeted. It is about 0.04% of a budget of roughly £1.2bn.

The £1.2bn covers the council's General Fund (its main budget for running services), its housing revenue account (the separate, ring-fenced account for council-owned homes, paid for by rents) and its capital programme (planned spending on things that last, such as buildings and roads).

The report says the 2025-26 final-quarter outturn "was presented to Cabinet in June, setting out a year-end underspend position of £0.483 million". The material available does not break the figure down by service or say what produced it.

news_drafts.headline: Newcastle schools-funding deficit forecast to reach £17.153m by March 2027, with override extended to 2028
news_drafts.lead:
Newcastle City Council expects the deficit on its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) to reach £17.153m by the end of 2026-27, according to the first-quarter outturn report (the forecast of the year's actual figures) put to Cabinet on 21 September. The grant is projecting an overspend of £11.297m this year, on top of a negative balance of £5.808m at 1 April 2026.

The overspend is in high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Spending there is forecast at £66.6m against funding of £55.2m. The paper puts spending growth at 15%, against 7% growth in funding.

For now the deficit does not touch the council's main budget. A statutory override (a temporary government rule that lets councils keep a schools-funding deficit off their main balance sheet) lets the council record it as an unusable reserve. The override was due to expire in March 2026, and the government has extended it to March 2028. The government is also offering a High Needs Stability Grant, covering up to 90% of eligible deficits, but it depends on the Department for Education approving a plan to reform support for children with special educational needs.
